HVAC&R System Design. One-shot notes, then every shortlisted past-paper topic (2020-2024) with full answers, slide figures and worked numericals. Your place, theme and text size are remembered on this device.

24-hour priority list

You answer 3 of 4 questions in each part, so each part has its own list. Study down both lists until the green pass line: about 6 h for Part A and 5 h for Part B, which leaves time for sleep and a last read of the one-shot notes. Alternate between parts (A block 1, B block 1, A block 2 …) so neither is left short. Chance: how often the topic came up, newer papers weigh more (2024 ×4, 2023 ×3, 2021 ×2, 2020 ×1). Covered: share of that part's past-paper marks you have studied once you finish the row.

Next if you have time: A4 in Part A (R22 80 kW numerical, asked word for word in 2021 and 2024) and B3 in Part B (summer AC with bypass factor, 15 marks in 2021 and 2024). Both sit just below the pass line but repeat almost unchanged, so they are the best extra hour in each part.

★ One-shot notes

Every definition, formula and numerical recipe in one place. Read this first and again the night before.

Section A: Refrigeration

Units and basics

Refrigeration: removing heat from a substance under controlled conditions and keeping it below the surroundings' temperature.

1 TR = melting 1 tonne ice from and at 0 °C in 24 h = 232.6 kJ/min; practice: 210 kJ/min = 3.5 kW.

COP = RE/W = (h1 − h4)/(h2 − h1); COP_HP = COP_R + 1 Carnot COP_R = TL/(TH − TL)

Refrigerator: wants QL (cold side). Heat pump: wants QH (hot side). Refrigeration controls temperature only; AC controls temperature + humidity + air motion + purity.

Ice / product load recipe

Q = m[cΔT + latent] / time(min) ÷ 210 = TR ice latent 335 kJ/kg, water c = 4.187, 1 t ice/day = 3.88 kW

2000 kg, 0→45 °C: 3.46 TR · 1500 kg, 0→25 °C: 2.18 TR · 600 kg fruit 25→−5 °C in 8 h (c 1.255, L 105): 0.85 TR

VCR cycle (C-C-E-E)

1→2Compressor, isentropic, w = h2 − h1
2→3Condenser, const p, q = h2 − h3
3→4Expansion valve, h4 = h3 (throttling)
4→1Evaporator, RE = h1 − h4

Throttle replaces turbine; dry vapour compressed (Carnot impractical: wet compression, wet expansion).

Dry sat. after compression: s1 = s2 = sg2; x1 = (s1 − sf1)/(sg1 − sf1); h1 = hf1 + x1hfg1.

Subcooling: RE ↑, W same → COP ↑ always. Superheat: RE ↑ and W ↑; COP may go either way; protects compressor.

Effect of temperatures

Tevap ↑ → RE ↑, W ↓, v1 ↓ (capacity ↑) → COP ↑. Tcond ↑ → RE ↓, W ↑, discharge temp ↑ → COP ↓.

Evaporator temp has more influence: ∂COP/∂Te = Tc/ΔT² > Te/ΔT². R22 example: +5 K evap → 4.13, −5 K cond → 4.11 (base 3.61).

R22 numerical recipe

find p_e, p_c; h1 (with superheat), v1, s1 h2 at p_c with s2 = s1; h3 = h_f(Tc − subcool) = h4 m = Q/(h1−h4); V = m·v1; P = m(h2−h1)

80 kW, −10/45 °C, 5 K sub, 10 K sup: h1 408.2, h2 450.4, h4 249.6, v1 0.0686 → m 0.505 kg/s, V 0.0346 m³/s, COP 3.75, P 21.3 kW.

2020 table (50 kW, 35/−10, h2 435.2): h1 401.06, h3 243.14 → RE 157.9, m 0.317, P 10.8 kW, COP 4.63.

Ammonia ice plant recipe

Q = tonnes × 3.88 kW. x1 from s, h1, COPth = (h1 − hf3)/(h2 − h1), × %, P = Q/COP.

25 t, 15/−5, 45%: COPth 12.8 → 16.9 kW. 30 t, 20/−10, 55%: 8.15 → 26.0 kW. Slide: 30 t, 25/−15, 60% → 33.2 kW.

Multistage

When: Tc − Te > 40 K (Gosney), high pressure ratio. Single stage then has: big cylinder, high discharge temp (oil burns), low ηvol, high friction/cost.

Advantages: less work, better ηvol, low discharge temp, more RE, less leakage, uniform torque, cheaper compressor. Disadvantages: cost, complexity.

p_i = √(p_c · p_e)

Flash cooler: LP comp 1→2, mix with flash gas → 3, HP comp → 4, condense → 5, valve 1 → 6 in flash chamber, vapour 7 to HP, liquid 8 → valve 2 → 9 evaporator. Flash gas skips evaporator and LP stage.

Single comp + multiple exp. valves: E3→E2→E1 in series, back-pressure valves, vapours mix to one compressor. Individual compressors: each evaporator has own compressor; COP higher.

Refrigerants

Criteria: thermodynamic, environmental & safety, economic.

Thermo: suction p above atm, low discharge p, low pressure ratio, high latent heat, low isentropic index, low liquid cp, high vapour cp, high k, low viscosity.

Environment: ODP = 0 (R11 = 1, Cl/Br destroy ozone), low GWP (CO2 = 1), low TEWI (direct leakage + indirect energy CO2).

Safety: non-toxic, non-flammable, chemically stable, compatible, oil miscible (NH3 no, R12 yes, R22 partly), easy leak detection. ASHRAE A/B toxicity, 1/2/3 flammability.

Compressors

Classes: method (recip, rotary, centrifugal), strokes (single/double acting), stages, drive (direct/belt), prime mover (open, semi-hermetic, hermetic).

Hermetic: motor + compressor on one shaft in one welded shell; no shaft seal. +: no leakage, quiet, compact, simple lubrication. −: inaccessible, separate pump for charging, burnout contaminates.

Centrifugal vs recip +: no valves/pistons (long life), no vibration, quiet, 3000+ rpm direct drive, big volumes, 50-5000 TR, high efficiency, less floor area. −: surging <35% load, not below 50 TR.

Absorption (VAR)

Compressor replaced by absorber + pump + generator (heat input). Pairs: H2O-LiBr (AC, >0 °C), NH3-H2O (below 0 °C).

SingleDoubleTriple
Generators12 (HTG vapour heats LTG)3
COP0.71.0-1.21.5-1.7
Heat80-120 °C150-170 °C200+ °C

VAR vs VCR: heat vs work; low vs high COP; few vs many moving parts; part load fine vs drops; quiet; bulky small units; good where waste heat is cheap.

Heat sources: steam, hot water, direct gas/oil firing, waste heat/exhaust, solar, geothermal.

LiBr problems: crystallization, air leakage (vacuum, purge), corrosion (inhibitors), freezing below ~4 °C, large vapour volume.

Practical plant performance

Full load: COP, EER, kW/ton. Part load: SEER, IPLV/NPLV.

EER = Btu/h ÷ W; COP = EER/3.412; kW/ton = 12/EER IPLV = 0.01A + 0.42B + 0.45C + 0.12D (100/75/50/25%)

HSPF = heating season Btu ÷ Wh (heat pumps). Energy Star = EPA efficiency label.

Other short answers

Air cycle: compress → cool → expand in turbine → absorb; COP = 1/(rp(γ−1)/γ − 1). Aircraft (2020): Q = 50 × 1 × 35 = 1750 kJ/min = 8.33 TR, COP ≈ 0.19.

TEV: bulb pressure opens; evaporator + spring pressure close; constant superheat.

Thermoelectric: Peltier, p-n couples; reverse current swaps hot and cold; COP 0.3-0.7. Magnetocaloric not commercial: costly magnets and Gd, small ΔT, low power density.

Cooling tower: natural/mechanical (forced, induced), counter/cross-flow. Range = in − out; Approach = out − WBT; ε = R/(R + A).

Linde: compress ~200 bar, HX regenerative cooling, J-T throttling, separate liquid; y = (h1 − h2)/(h1 − hf).

Psychrometric definitions

WBTlowest temp by evaporating water; wet wick in moving air; DBT − WBT = depression
DPTtemp where vapour starts condensing on cooling at constant p (constant w)
wkg vapour/kg dry air = 0.622 pv/(pt − pv)

Saturated air: DBT = WBT = DPT. Always DBT ≥ WBT ≥ DPT.

SHF line: join chart reference point (26 °C, 50%) to SHF on protractor, draw parallel through room point. tanθ = (1/2451)(1 − SHF)/SHF.

Processes and air washer

Sensible heat/cool: w constant (coil above DPT). Cool + dehumidify: coil below DPT; mw = ma(wo − wc), Q = ma(ho − hc). Heat + humidify: heating coil then steam/spray.

Qs = m·cpm·Δt QL = m·2501·Δw Qt = m·Δh

DPT-WBTcool + humidify (cool water)

Air washer = spray chamber + eliminators + pump + cooler/heater + make-up water. ηH = 1 − X.

Summer AC + ventilation + BPF recipe

mix: t1 = r·ti + (1−r)to (same for w, h) coil: ts = ADP + X(t1 − ADP) m_d = RSH / [1.02(ti − ts)] m_o = (OA share)·m_d OASH = m_o·1.02(to−ti) OALH = m_o·2500(wo−wi) GTH = RSH + RLH + m_o(ho − hi) ; TR = GTH/3.5

RSHF line: room i → supply. GSHF line: mixed 1 → coil ADP. ADP unknown? Try ADP until 1.02(ti − ts)/[2501(wi − ws)] = RSH/RLH.

2024: md 1.83 kg/s, OASH 8.4, OALH 8.0, GTH 41.8 kW. 2021 (OA 35 °C/65%): ADP 11.5 °C, 46.4 cmm, 91.1 kW. Slide ex. (4:1, X 0.1): 1.73 kg/s, 37.7 kW.

Thermal comfort

Def: condition of mind expressing satisfaction with the thermal environment. Factors: air temp, MRT, RH, air velocity, activity (met), clothing (clo).

Comfort chart: ET lines + 60% RH top + 2 °C DPT bottom. Winter ET 20-23.5 °C, summer 22.5-26 °C, 1.2 met.

ET: temp of standard 50% RH environment giving the same skin heat loss. Operative: (ta + tmrt)/2, radiation + convection.

PPD = 100 − 95 exp(−0.03353PMV&sup4; − 0.2179PMV²); PMV 0 → PPD 5%

So nobody can satisfy everyone. Indoor design: 24-26 °C, 50-60%. Outdoor design: statistical 1-2.5% weather values.

IAQ

SBS (symptoms vanish outside) vs BRI (real disease, persists). 90% time indoors; indoor air 2-5× worse.

Control: 1. Source control (low-VOC, intakes 8-10 ft high, 10-15 ft from exhausts, RH < 60%) 2. Filtration (MERV: panel 1-4, pleated 5-8, bag 9-15; HEPA 99.97% at 0.3 μm; ULPA 99.999% at 0.12 μm) 3. Dilution (ventilation, CO2 sensor).

V = n·Np / (C_in − C_out); Np = 0.011 cfm CO2; C_in 1000 ppm 1 person, 300 ppm out: 15.7 cfm

30 students: Khulna (400) 550 cfm = 0.26 m³/s; Dhaka (800) 1650 cfm = 0.78 m³/s (3×).

AC systems

Zone: space(s) controlled by one thermostat. Split: indoor evaporator + blower, outdoor compressor + condenser, two pipes.

All-air: single-duct CAV, CAV reheat, multizone, dual duct, VAV. +: central plant, good humidity/filtration, economizer, quiet. −: big ducts, fan energy.

Dual duct CAV: one fan, hot + cold ducts, mixing box per zone; constant air, variable temperature.

CAV vs VAV: fixed air/variable temp vs fixed temp/variable air; VAV saves fan energy.

Rooftop: + packaged, saves floor space, quick; − roof load, weather, service access.

Choice matrix (2024): Σ importance × score: split 346, rooftop 434.

VRF

Inverter compressor + EEV per indoor unit, one outdoor unit, many indoor units. +: part-load efficiency, zone control, heat recovery, no ducts, modular, quiet.

3-pipe heat recovery: discharge gas, suction gas, liquid. Heating unit: hot gas in → liquid out. Cooling unit: liquid in → suction gas out. 2-pipe: 2 pipes to a BC controller that separates gas/liquid.

Multi-split vs VRF: few units, own pipes, same mode, short pipes vs up to 60 units, shared branches, simultaneous heat/cool, long pipes, EEV.

Cooling load

Cooling: unsteady, daytime peak, internal gains added. Heating: steady, pre-dawn peak, no sun or internal gains.

Assumptions: statistical outdoor design data, clear sky, full occupancy, equipment at representative capacity, near-max not max.

opaque: U·A·CLTD(ETD) floor/basement: U·A·(To−Ti) glass: A[Ug(To−Ti) + SHGF·SC·CLF] infil: m = ρ·ACH·Vol/3600; m·cpm·ΔT + m·2501·ΔW people: N×S×CLF + N×L ; lights: W×UF×BF(1.25)×CLF GTH = RSH + RLH + OATH; ×1.25 safety

2024 room: RSH 5035 W, RLH 578 W, ×1.25 = 7.0 kW ≈ 2 TR (glass U 3.12 assumed, inside 25 °C/50%).

Sol-air temp: tsa = to + αI/ho − εΔR/ho. Infiltration: uncontrolled leakage; crack method = crack length × leakage per m; or ACH method.

Rules: short and straight, low aspect ratio (≤4:1), velocity limits for noise, gradual transitions, sealed and insulated, dampers for balancing.

Outlet location: throw/spread/drop, near heat sources (windows), no short-circuit to returns, noise, ceiling height. Dampers control/balance flow; diffusers spread and slow supply air.

A3 Ton of refrigeration, COP and ice / cold-storage load Very likely · 100%Easy

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2024 Q1(a) [10] Define Ton. Calculate the refrigeration tonnage for 2000 kg ice melting from 0 °C to 45 °C.
  • 2023 Q1(d) [7] Calculate the refrigeration tonnage for 1500 kg ice from 0 °C to 25 °C.
  • 2021 Q1(a) [8] Define Ton and COP (coefficient of performance) of refrigeration system. What is the basic difference between a refrigerator and a heat pump?
  • 2020 Q1(a) [8] What is meant by TR (ton of refrigeration (3.5 kW))? Write down the differences between refrigeration and air conditioning system.
  • 2020 Q1(c) [10] 600 kg of fruits are supplied to a cold storage at 25 °C. The cold storage is maintained at −5 °C and the fruits get cooled to the storage temperature in 8 hours. The latent heat of freezing is 105 kJ/kg and specific heat of fruit is 1.255 kJ/kgK. Find the refrigeration capacity of the plant.
Before you start: ton of refrigeration and ice load

1 TR = cooling needed to freeze (or melt) 1 tonne of ice at 0 °C in 24 hours ≈ 3.5 kW = 210 kJ/min.

Heat to change ice/water: latent heat (melting or freezing, no temperature change) = m × 335 kJ/kg; sensible heat (temperature change) = m × c × ΔT, with c = 4.187 kJ/kg·K for water, about 2.1 for ice.

Definitions (2020 1a, 2021 1a, 2024 1a)

Refrigeration is the process of removing heat from a substance under controlled conditions and keeping it below the temperature of its surroundings.

Ton of refrigeration (TR): the refrigerating effect produced by the uniform melting of 1 tonne (1000 kg) of ice from and at 0 °C in 24 hours.

1 TR = 1000 × 335 kJ / 24 h = 232.6 kJ/min ≈ 210 kJ/min = 3.5 kW (value used in practice)

COP = heat extracted / work done = refrigerating effect / compressor work = (h1 − h4)/(h2 − h1)

Refrigerator vs heat pump
RefrigeratorHeat pump
Purpose: remove heat QL from the cold spacePurpose: supply heat QH to the warm space
COPR = QL/WCOPHP = QH/W = COPR + 1
Useful side: evaporatorUseful side: condenser

Same device and same cycle; only the objective differs.

Refrigeration vs air conditioning (2020 1a)
RefrigerationAir conditioning
Controls only temperature (usually below ambient)Controls temperature, humidity, air motion and air purity together
Applied to products: food, ice, medicine, processApplied mainly to human comfort or industrial spaces
Space may be far below 0 °CSpace kept near 20-26 °C
Refrigeration is a part of ACAC uses refrigeration plus heating, humidifying, filtering, fans
Numerical 1 (2024 1a): 2000 kg ice, 0 °C to 45 °C

Read as: 2000 kg of ice at 0 °C melts and the water is warmed to 45 °C in 24 h (making ice from water at 45 °C gives the same answer).

Latent heat = 2000 × 335 = 670 000 kJ

Sensible heat = 2000 × 4.187 × (45 − 0) = 376 830 kJ

Total Q = 1 046 830 kJ per day = 1 046 830 / 1440 = 727.0 kJ/min

Tonnage = 727.0 / 210 = 3.46 TR

Numerical 2 (2023 1d): 1500 kg ice, 0 °C to 25 °C

Q = 1500 [335 + 4.187 × 25] = 1500 × 439.7 = 659 550 kJ/day

= 659 550 / 1440 = 458.0 kJ/min

Tonnage = 458.0 / 210 = 2.18 TR

Numerical 3 (2020 1c): 600 kg fruit, 25 °C to −5 °C in 8 h

Sensible heat = m c ΔT = 600 × 1.255 × (25 − (−5)) = 22 590 kJ

Latent heat of freezing = 600 × 105 = 63 000 kJ

Total = 85 590 kJ in 8 h = 85 590 / 480 = 178.3 kJ/min

Capacity = 178.3 / 210 = 0.85 TR

Remember: Load (kJ) ÷ time (min) ÷ 210 = TR. Ice: 335 kJ/kg latent, water 4.187 kJ/kg K.

Same answer, step by step with reasons
Step (write this)Why / what it means
2024: Latent = 2000 × 335 = 670,000 kJMelting the ice at 0 °C (no temperature change).
Sensible = 2000 × 4.187 × 45 = 376,830 kJWarming the water from 0 to 45 °C.
Total = 1,046,830 kJ per day ÷ 1440 min = 727 kJ/min24 h = 1440 min.
TR = 727 / 210 = 3.46 TR1 TR = 210 kJ/min.
2023: 1500 × (335 + 4.187 × 25) / 1440 / 210 = 2.18 TRSame recipe in one line.

Memory trick: "Latent + Sensible, per minute, over 210".

A7 Compressors: hermetic sealed, classification Very likely · 100%Easy

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2024 Q3(d) [5] Write down the advantages and disadvantages of hermetic sealed compressor.
  • 2024 Q3(c) [7] Classify compressors. Write down the advantages of centrifugal compressors over reciprocating compressors.
  • 2023 Q3(c) [8] What is meant by hermetic sealed compressor? Write down its advantages and disadvantages.
  • 2021 Q3(d) [10] What is meant by hermetic sealed compressor? What are the advantages and disadvantages of this compressor?
  • 2020 Q3(b) [7] What is meant by hermetic sealed compressor? What are its advantages?
Before you start: compressors

The compressor is the heart of the system. Reciprocating (piston), rotary, scroll, screw and centrifugal types exist. Hermetic = motor and compressor sealed together in one welded shell (no shaft seal, no leaks; household fridges and ACs).

Hermetic sealed compressor

When the compressor and the motor run on the same shaft and are enclosed in a common welded casing, it is a hermetic sealed compressor. It removes the crankshaft seal that an open compressor needs to stop refrigerant leakage. It can be reciprocating or rotary, vertical or horizontal; used in household refrigerators and window/split ACs. Suction gas cools the motor windings.

AdvantagesDisadvantages
1. Leakage of refrigerant completely prevented (no shaft seal)1. Maintenance is not easy; moving parts are inaccessible (shell must be cut)
2. Less noisy2. A separate pump is needed for evacuation and charging
3. Small space; compact3. Motor burnout contaminates the whole system
4. Simple lubrication; motor and compressor in sealed oil space4. Speed cannot be changed; limited to small capacities
5. Cheaper for small units; no belt or coupling5. Motor heat is added to the refrigerant

Items 1-4 in each column are from the slides; the rest are standard textbook points to add if more marks are needed.

Classification of compressors (2024 3c)
  1. Method of compression: reciprocating, rotary, centrifugal
  2. Working strokes: single acting, double acting
  3. Number of stages: single stage, multi-stage
  4. Method of drive: direct drive, belt drive
  5. Location of prime mover: open, semi-hermetic, hermetic
Advantages of centrifugal over reciprocating
  1. No valves, pistons, cylinders or connecting rods, so longer working life.
  2. Little or no vibration, since there are no unbalanced masses.
  3. Quiet and calm operation.
  4. High speed (3000 rpm and above), so they couple directly to electric motors or steam turbines.
  5. Handle large volumes of vapour.
  6. Suited to 50-5000 TR (ton of refrigeration (3.5 kW)) systems and −90 °C to +10 °C.
  7. High efficiency.
  8. Large units need less floor area.

Disadvantages: surging below about 35% load, low pressure rise per stage, not practical below 50 TR, needs refrigerants with high specific volume.

Remember: Hermetic = one sealed shell: no leak, quiet, compact; but no access, no repair.

A6 Refrigerant selection: environmental and safety properties Very likely · 100%Easy

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2024 Q3(b) [10] What are the major criteria of refrigerant selection? Explain the environmental and safety properties of a good refrigerant.
  • 2023 Q3(b) [8] Discuss the environmental and safety properties to consider before selecting a refrigerant.
  • 2021 Q2(b) [8] Briefly discuss the desirable characteristics of a fluid to be used as a refrigerant.
  • 2020 Q2(a) [7] Explain the environmental and safety properties of refrigerant.
Before you start: what makes a good refrigerant

It must boil at a low temperature at a reasonable pressure, carry a lot of heat per kg, and be safe: not toxic, not flammable, and not harmful to the ozone layer (low ODP (ozone depletion potential)) or climate (low GWP (global warming potential)). Old CFCs like R12 damaged ozone; R22 (HCFC) is being phased out; R134a, R410A, R32, ammonia, CO2 and hydrocarbons are used now.

What is a refrigerant

The working fluid that absorbs heat by evaporating at low temperature and pressure and rejects heat by condensing at higher temperature and pressure. Primary refrigerants (R134a, NH3, R22) run the cycle; secondary refrigerants (brine, chilled water) carry cold from the plant to the load.

Major selection criteria (2024 3b)
  1. Thermodynamic and thermo-physical properties
  2. Environmental and safety properties
  3. Economics (cheap, easily available)
Desirable thermodynamic properties (2021 2b)
PropertyShould beReason
Suction (evaporator) pressureAbove atmospheric, highNo air/moisture ingress, easy leak detection, small compressor
Discharge pressureLowLight compressor and condenser
Pressure ratioSmallHigh volumetric efficiency, low power
Latent heat of vaporizationLargeSmall mass flow per kW
Isentropic indexSmallLow discharge temperature
Liquid specific heatSmallMore subcooling, less flash gas
Vapour specific heatLargeLess superheating
Thermal conductivityHighBetter heat transfer
ViscosityLowLess pressure drop
Critical temperature / freezing pointWell outside working rangeCondensation possible; no freezing
Environmental properties (2024, 2023, 2020)
  • ODP (ozone depletion potential) should be zero (Montreal Protocol). Chlorine/bromine destroy ozone: CFCs (R11, R12) are phased out, HCFC (hydrochlorofluorocarbon) R22 is being phased out. Reference R11: ODP = 1.
  • GWP (global warming potential): climate impact of a gas compared with the same mass of CO2 (GWP = 1). Should be as low as possible; zero-ODP but high-GWP fluids such as R134a will be regulated.
  • TEWI (total equivalent warming impact) = direct effect (leakage, losses at recovery) + indirect effect (CO2 from the electricity used). Low TEWI is preferred.
Safety properties
  • Toxicity: should be non-toxic. Toxicity is relative: it matters only with the concentration and exposure time.
  • Flammability: should be non-flammable and non-explosive; flammable ones (HCs, NH3 partly) need special precautions. ASHRAE (American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers) classes: A/B = lower/higher toxicity, 1/2/3 = no/low/high flammability (R134a is A1, NH3 is B2L).
  • Chemical stability inside the system; compatibility with metals, gaskets and motor insulation.
  • Miscibility with oil: NH3 is not miscible (needs oil separator); R12 fully miscible; R22 partly (design for oil return).
  • Ease of leak detection. High dielectric strength (hermetic motors).

Remember: Environment = ODP, GWP, TEWI. Safety = Toxic, Flammable, Stable, Compatible, Oil, Leak (TF-SCOL).

A13 Thermoelectric, magnetocaloric and other novel cooling Very likely · 90%Easy

Past-paper questions · Good to have

  • 2024 Q8(a) [10] Explain the working principle of the thermoelectric cooling technique. How does reversing current affect its operation? (asked in Section B)
  • 2024 Q8(b) [10] Explain the reason why magneto-caloric cooling has not yet achieved commercial adoption in building HVAC (heating, ventilation and air-conditioning) system. (Section B)
  • 2023 Q4(d) [10] How thermo-electric cooling technique differs from solar-assisted cooling system? Explain which one is more efficient system and why?
  • 2021 Q3(b) [5] Differentiate between thermo-electric and electro-caloric cooling systems.
Before you start: novel cooling

Thermoelectric (Peltier): passing current through two different semiconductors moves heat from one junction to the other; no moving parts. Magnetocaloric: some materials heat up when magnetised and cool when demagnetised.

Not covered in the uploaded slides; written from standard textbooks (Arora, Khurmi). Check against class notes.

Thermoelectric cooling (2024 8a)
  • Based on the Peltier effect: when DC current flows through a junction of two dissimilar semiconductors (n-type and p-type, usually bismuth telluride), heat is absorbed at one junction and released at the other.
  • Many p-n couples are connected electrically in series and thermally in parallel between two ceramic plates: one plate gets cold (absorbs heat from the space), the other gets hot (rejects heat to a heat sink + fan).
  • Heat pumped Qc = αITc − ½I²R − KΔT.
  • Reversing the current swaps the hot and cold sides: the device becomes a heater instead of a cooler. So one unit can heat or cool just by switching polarity.
  • No moving parts or refrigerant, silent, compact, precise control; but low COP (0.3-0.7), used for small coolers, electronics, medical boxes.
Thermoelectric vs solar-assisted cooling (2023 4d)
ThermoelectricSolar-assisted (absorption/adsorption or PV-driven VCR (vapour compression refrigeration))
Electric (DC), Peltier effectUses solar heat (collectors driving VAR (vapour absorption refrigeration)/adsorption) or solar electricity
COP (coefficient of performance) 0.3-0.7Thermal COP 0.6-1.2 (VAR); PV + VCR overall COP high
Small capacity, no moving partsLarge capacity, needs collectors and storage

Solar-assisted cooling is more efficient for building loads: it uses free renewable heat and the absorption/VCR cycle has a much higher COP than Peltier modules, whose efficiency is limited by Joule heating and heat conduction back through the elements.

Thermoelectric vs electro-caloric (2021 3b)
ThermoelectricElectro-caloric
Peltier effect: current through a junction moves heatApplying an electric field to a dielectric (polymer/ceramic) orders its dipoles, so it heats up; removing the field cools it
Continuous DC currentCyclic field with heat regenerator
Commercial, low COPResearch stage, potentially higher efficiency
Why magnetocaloric cooling is not commercial in buildings (2024 8b)
  1. Needs strong magnetic fields (1-2 T) from rare-earth permanent magnets: heavy and expensive.
  2. Good magnetocaloric materials (gadolinium alloys) are costly and scarce.
  3. Small temperature change per cycle (2-5 K), so many regenerator stages and high cycle frequency are needed; capacity per kg is low.
  4. Hysteresis, fatigue and corrosion of materials in water-based fluid.
  5. Complex moving parts (rotating magnets), pumps and valves; poor heat transfer.
  6. Vapour compression is cheap and mature, so there is no cost case yet.

Remember: Peltier: reverse current = swap hot/cold. Magnetocaloric: costly magnets, small ΔT, low power density.

A2 Effect of evaporator and condenser temperature on COP Very likely · 90%Easy

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2024 Q2(a) [12] Discuss the effect of evaporating and condensing temperature on the cycle efficiency with necessary diagrams.
  • 2023 Q1(b) [10] Explain the effects of evaporating and condensing temperature on the performance of vapor compression refrigeration cycle.
  • 2021 Q1(b) [12] How does the increase in condenser temperature affect on COP (coefficient of performance)? Also briefly explain the influence of evaporator temperature on COP. Which of the two temperatures have more influence on COP?
Before you start: why temperatures change COP

COP (coefficient of performance) = heat removed / work input. The compressor has to lift the heat from the evaporator temperature up to the condenser temperature. The bigger that lift, the more work per kJ of cooling, so COP falls. Ideal (Carnot) COP = TL/(TH − TL) in kelvin shows it.

(1) Effect of evaporating temperature (condensing temperature fixed)
  • Refrigerating effect qo = h1 − h3 increases, because h1 (saturated vapour enthalpy) rises.
  • Compressor work w = h2 − h1 decreases, because the pressure lift is smaller.
  • Suction specific volume v1 falls a lot, so the volumetric refrigerating effect (h1 − h3)/v1 and capacity rise quickly.
  • So COP increases with higher evaporating temperature and falls sharply when it is lowered.

Lower suction pressure (from friction or low evaporator temperature) does the opposite: RE (refrigerating effect) falls from (h1 − h4) to (h1′ − h4′), work rises from (h2 − h1) to (h2′ − h1′), and COP decreases.

(2) Effect of condensing temperature (evaporating temperature fixed)
  • Lower condensing temperature: h3 drops, so RE increases; the pressure lift is smaller, so work decreases; heat rejected also decreases. COP increases.
  • Increase in condensing temperature (the 2021 question) has the opposite effect: RE falls from (h1 − h4) to (h1 − h4′), work rises from (h2 − h1) to (h2′ − h1), discharge temperature rises, and COP decreases.
Which one has more influence? (2021 1b)

The evaporator temperature has more influence on COP. From the Carnot COP = Te/(Tc − Te):

∂COP/∂Te = Tc/(Tc − Te)²  >  |∂COP/∂Tc| = Te/(Tc − Te)²   because Tc > Te

Raising the evaporator temperature also cuts v1 sharply, so capacity improves too. Example with R22 (ideal cycle, −10 °C / 45 °C, COP 3.61): raising te by 5 K gives COP 4.13, while lowering tc by 5 K gives 4.11.

Effect on cycle efficiency in one line (2024 2a)

The smaller the gap between condensing and evaporating temperatures, the higher the COP: keep the evaporator as warm and the condenser as cool as the application allows.

Remember: High evaporator, low condenser = high COP. Evaporator wins because Tc > Te.

A1 Vapour compression refrigeration (VCR) cycle Very likely · 80%Easy

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2024 Q1(b) [12] Explain thermodynamic process of an ideal vapor compression refrigeration (VCR) cycle with necessary sketches.
  • 2023 Q1(a) [10] Describe the working principle of vapor compression refrigeration system with neat sketch.
  • 2020 Q1(b) [12] Discuss about the thermodynamic process of theoretical vapor compression refrigeration cycle with dry saturated vapor after compression with necessary diagrams.
Before you start: how a fridge moves heat

Heat naturally flows from hot to cold. A refrigerator pushes it the other way using a liquid (refrigerant) that boils at a very low temperature. In the evaporator (inside the fridge) it boils and absorbs heat; the compressor squeezes the vapour so it becomes hot; in the condenser (outside, at the back) it gives that heat to the room and turns back to liquid; the expansion valve drops its pressure so it is cold again.

Enthalpy h (kJ/kg) = energy content per kg of refrigerant. On a p-h chart every process is a straight line, so all answers come from four h values.

Components and schematic

The VCR (vapour compression refrigeration) system has four components: compressor, condenser, expansion valve, evaporator. The refrigerant enters the compressor as saturated vapour, leaves the condenser as saturated liquid, is throttled to evaporator pressure, and evaporates by absorbing heat from the cold space.

The four processes (state points 1-2-3-4)
ProcessWhereWhat happensEnergy per kg
1→2CompressorIsentropic compression of dry vapour from pe to pc; becomes superheated (or dry saturated)w = h2 − h1
2→3CondenserConstant-pressure heat rejection: desuperheat then condense to saturated liquidqc = h2 − h3
3→4Expansion valveThrottling, no heat or work; pressure and temperature drop, part flashes to vapourh4 = h3
4→1EvaporatorConstant-pressure evaporation; absorbs heat from the spaceRE (refrigerating effect) = h1 − h4

COP (coefficient of performance) = RE / w = (h1 − h4) / (h2 − h1)    Qe = m (h1 − h4)    P = m (h2 − h1)

Why not the reversed Carnot cycle?

Carnot would need compression of a wet mixture (2 phases in the compressor) and expansion in a turbine of a very wet fluid. Both are impractical, so the ideal VCR cycle compresses dry vapour and uses a throttle valve instead of a turbine; the small work lost is not worth the cost of a turbine.

Cycle with dry saturated vapour after compression (2020 1b)

Here state 1 is wet (dryness x1) so that isentropic compression ends exactly on the saturated vapour line at state 2 (s1 = s2 = sg2). Then condensation 2→3 is only latent heat at constant temperature T2 = T3.

h1 = hf1 + x1 hfg1, with x1 from s1 = sf1 + x1(sg1 − sf1) = sg2;   COP = (h1 − hf3)/(h2 − h1)

Subcooling and superheating (often asked with the cycle)
  • Subcooling cools the liquid below saturation (3→3′). RE rises by h3 − h3′, work is unchanged, so COP always rises.
  • Superheating (1→1′) increases both RE and work; COP may rise, fall or stay the same. Some superheat protects the compressor from liquid; too much overheats oil.

Remember: C-C-E-E: Compress (w = h2−h1), Condense, Expand (h4 = h3), Evaporate (RE = h1−h4).

A8 Vapour absorption (VAR): single, double, triple effect Very likely · 100%Medium

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2024 Q4(b) [13] Describe the commercial double-effect VAR (vapour absorption refrigeration) system with necessary sketch.
  • 2024 Q4(c) [8] Briefly explain the different heat sources of VAR system.
  • 2023 Q3(a) [13] Write down the classification of vapor absorption refrigeration system. Describe the triple effect vapor absorption system with a schematic diagram.
  • 2023 Q3(d) [6] Differentiate between VCR (vapour compression refrigeration) and VAR systems.
  • 2021 Q4(d) [10] Draw the schematic of a single effect absorption refrigeration system. Also explain how it is different from double effect absorption refrigeration system.
  • 2021 Q4(b) [6] What are the advantages of vapor absorption system over vapor compression refrigeration system?
  • 2020 Q3(a) [10] Draw double effect absorption refrigeration system and explain how it is different from triple effect absorption refrigeration system.
Before you start: absorption refrigeration

Instead of a compressor, an absorption system uses heat (steam, hot water, gas flame, waste heat). The refrigerant vapour is absorbed into a liquid (water absorbs ammonia; lithium bromide solution absorbs water vapour), pumped up as liquid (very little work), then boiled out again in a generator by heat. Double and triple effect reuse the generator heat in more stages for higher COP (coefficient of performance).

Before you start: why absorption can replace the compressor

In a normal (VCR) refrigerator, the compressor has one job: take the cold, low-pressure vapour from the evaporator and push it up to the high pressure of the condenser. Squeezing a gas needs a lot of work (electricity).

Pumping a liquid to the same pressure needs almost no work, because a liquid hardly changes volume. So VAR plays a trick: first dissolve the vapour into a liquid (absorber), pump the liquid up to high pressure, then boil the vapour back out with heat (generator). Absorber + pump + generator = a "thermal compressor".

Everyday picture: salt or silica gel soaks up moisture from air (absorber). Heat the wet salt and the water steams out again (generator). The salt is reused.

Side note: Working pair. Water is the refrigerant (it does the cooling). Lithium bromide (LiBr), a salt, is the absorbent: it loves water and never boils off, so only pure water vapour leaves the generator. Water boils at 5 °C only under a deep vacuum (about 0.9 kPa), so the low side of a LiBr (lithium bromide) machine is a vacuum. For temperatures below 0 °C the pair is ammonia (refrigerant) + water (absorbent).

1. Single-effect system: one generator (2021 4d)
  1. Evaporator (low pressure, ~0.9 kPa): liquid water boils at about 5 °C and takes heat Qe from the chilled water. This is the cooling effect.
  2. Absorber (same low pressure): strong LiBr solution sprays over tubes and soaks up the water vapour. Absorbing releases heat Qa, removed by cooling water (a cool solution absorbs better). The solution becomes weak (watery).
  3. Pump: lifts the weak solution to the high pressure. Little work, since it is liquid.
  4. Heat exchanger: hot strong solution coming back preheats the cold weak solution going up. Saves generator heat.
  5. Generator (high pressure, ~7.4 kPa): heat Qg (steam, hot water, waste heat) boils water vapour out of the solution. The solution becomes strong again and returns through the heat exchanger and a valve to the absorber.
  6. Condenser → expansion valve → evaporator: the vapour condenses (Qc out), drops in pressure through the valve and enters the evaporator. Same as VCR.

COPVAR = Qe / (Qg + Wpump) ≈ Qe/Qg ≈ 0.7 for single effect

Side note: Why COP is below 1: to boil 1 kg of water out of the solution the generator must supply about its latent heat (plus some heat of mixing). That 1 kg then gives about the same latent heat of cooling in the evaporator. So cooling out ≈ heat in, minus losses, which gives about 0.7. Do not compare this with a VCR COP of 3-4: VAR is fed cheap heat, VCR is fed expensive electricity.

2. Double-effect system: use the heat twice (2024 4b, 2020 3a, 2021 4d)
Before you start: the one idea behind double effect

In single effect, the hot vapour from the generator goes to the condenser and all its latent heat is thrown away into cooling water. That is wasted energy.

Fix: run the first generator at a higher pressure, so its vapour is hotter (it condenses at about 90 °C instead of 40 °C). Then let that vapour condense inside the tubes of a second, low-temperature generator. Its latent heat boils more water out there. One fuel input, about twice the refrigerant vapour, so about twice the cooling.

Full double-effect schematic (for the exam sketch)
  1. Weak solution from the absorber is pumped through the LT and HT heat exchangers to the high-temperature generator (HTG).
  2. Steam (~8 bar) or a gas burner heats the HTG to about 150 °C. Vapour 1 is boiled off. The solution leaves as medium strength.
  3. Vapour 1 goes into the tubes of the low-temperature generator (LTG) and condenses there. Its latent heat boils vapour 2 out of the medium solution. No extra fuel.
  4. Vapour 2 goes to the condenser. The condensed vapour 1 (now liquid) also goes to the condenser. Both then pass the expansion valve to the evaporator.
  5. Strong solution from the LTG returns through the heat exchangers to the absorber. Evaporator and absorber work as in single effect.

COP ≈ 1.0-1.2: about 70 % higher than single effect, so steam use is roughly halved.

3. Triple-effect system: use the heat three times (2023 3a, 2020 3a)

Same idea once more. Add a third, even hotter generator on top (about 200 °C solution, about 4 bar). Its vapour heats generator 2, whose vapour heats generator 1, whose vapour goes to the condenser. One heat input, three boilings.

  • COP ≈ 1.4-1.7.
  • Needs 200-230 °C heat, so it is direct fired (gas).
  • Higher temperature and pressure make LiBr very corrosive and the solution may crystallize (turn to solid salt and block pipes). Special materials and controls are needed, so it is expensive and rare.
4. COP trend and comparison
Single effectDouble effectTriple effect
Generators12 (HTG + LTG)3
Pressure levels234
Times the heat is usedoncetwicethree times
Heat source80-120 °C hot water, low-pressure steam, waste heat150-170 °C steam (~8 bar) or gas burner200-230 °C, direct fired
COP≈ 0.7≈ 1.0-1.2≈ 1.4-1.7
Problemslow COP, big cooling towercost, corrosionhigh pressure, severe corrosion and crystallization, very costly, few units
Usewaste heat, solar, hot watermost common commercial chillerspecial / research, gas-fired
5. Diagrams: Dühring (p-T) chart and p-h chart
Before you start: which chart is used for VAR

A VAR has two fluids: pure water (refrigerant) and LiBr solution. A p-h chart of water can only show the refrigerant side: condenser, valve, evaporator. The absorber and generator work on the solution, so textbooks use the Dühring chart: ln p on the vertical axis and −1/T on the horizontal axis (labelled in °C). On it, pure water and every LiBr concentration plot as almost straight lines, so the whole cycle is a few straight lines.

How to read it: a point to the right of the water line at the same pressure is solution that is hotter than pure water at that pressure. That is why the absorber at 0.9 kPa can sit at 40 °C while water boils at 5 °C.

Show:

Tap a dot. Each dot explains one component. Use the buttons to add the second and third effect.

Side note: How to sketch it in the exam (2 minutes): draw two horizontal lines for low pressure (evaporator/absorber) and high pressure (condenser/generator). Draw the water line on the left and two solution lines (weak, strong) to the right. Put evaporator and condenser on the water line, absorber and generator on the solution lines, and join them. For double effect add one more pressure level on top, for triple effect add two.

Show:

Tap a point. Each point explains the state of the water.

Write this in the exam (double or triple effect, 5-7 marks)
  1. Sketch the schematic (or the effect ladder) with generators, condenser, evaporator, absorber, pump, heat exchangers.
  2. One line of principle: "Vapour from the higher-temperature generator condenses in the next generator and supplies its heat, so the same heat input generates refrigerant vapour two (three) times."
  3. State the working pair (H2O-LiBr), the source temperature and the COP (0.7 / 1.2 / 1.6).
  4. Add the Dühring sketch with 3 (double) or 4 (triple) pressure levels.
  5. One advantage (higher COP, half the steam) and one drawback (higher temperature, corrosion, crystallization, cost).

Memory trick: "1-2-3 generators, 0.7-1.2-1.7 COP, 90-150-200 °C." Each extra effect = one more generator on top, COP up by 0.5, source about 50 K hotter. Think of a waterfall turning wheels: the heat falls through each generator in turn, and every wheel it turns makes more cold.

Double and triple effect details are from standard textbooks (Arora, ASHRAE (American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers)), since the uploaded slides only cover single effect. Temperatures and pressures are typical rounded values.

VCR vs VAR (2023 3d)
Advantages of VAR over VCR (2021 4b)
  1. Runs on low-grade heat (waste heat, solar, steam), so lower operating cost where heat is cheap.
  2. Few moving parts (only a pump): quiet, less vibration and maintenance.
  3. Uses natural refrigerants (water, ammonia); no CFCs.
  4. Performance hardly falls at part load; COP not sensitive to evaporator temperature.
  5. Liquid at evaporator exit is not a problem (no compressor to damage).
  6. Large capacities are economical; useful for heat recovery.
Heat sources of VAR (2024 4c)
  • Steam (low pressure for single effect, ~8 bar for double effect)
  • Hot water from boilers or district heating
  • Direct firing of natural gas or oil
  • Waste heat: engine jacket water, exhaust gases, process heat, cogeneration
  • Solar thermal collectors; geothermal water

Remember: VAR = heat in, pump instead of compressor. Each extra generator reuses the heat: COP 0.7 → 1.2 → 1.6.

A5 Multistage / multipressure systems and flash cooler Very likely · 100%Medium

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2024 Q3(a) [13] Why and when multi-stage VCR (vapour compression refrigeration) system is required? Explain two-stage expansion system with a flash cooler with necessary sketch.
  • 2023 Q2(a) [10] Why multi-stage vapor compression is required? Write down the advantages and disadvantages of a multi-stage vapor compression system.
  • 2023 Q2(b) [13] Describe two-stage expansion system with a flash cooler with necessary diagrams.
  • 2021 Q2(a) [12] What is meant by multipressure systems? Discuss about the individual compressors-multiple expansion valves with the required diagrams.
  • 2020 Q2(b) [11] Define multistage compression. Explain the single compressor-multiple expansion valves with the required p-h diagram.
Before you start: why multistage

If the evaporator is very cold and the condenser hot, one compressor has to work across a huge pressure ratio: it gets hot, inefficient, and much of the liquid flashes to vapour in the expansion valve. Splitting compression into two stages with an intercooler and a flash chamber (which removes the flash vapour at intermediate pressure) saves work.

Why and when multistage is needed

A single stage works well when the pressure ratio between condenser and evaporator is moderate. A limit of about 40 K between condensing and evaporating temperature is recommended (Gosney); above that, use multistage (or cascade) systems. With a large pressure ratio (very low evaporator or high condenser temperature), a single stage suffers:

  1. Cylinder size becomes too large.
  2. Discharge temperature becomes very high; it may heat the cylinder head or burn the lubricating oil.
  3. Heat cannot be rejected in the short compression time.
  4. Friction losses and running cost are high.
  5. Volumetric efficiency is low.

Multipressure system: a system with two or more low-side pressures (several evaporators at different temperatures) or with compression in stages, giving more than one pressure level between pe and pc.

Advantages of multistage compression
  1. Less work per kg (with intercooling) for the same delivery pressure.
  2. Lower compression ratio per stage, so better volumetric and compressor efficiency.
  3. Lower discharge temperature; better lubrication.
  4. Liquid enters the evaporator at lower enthalpy, so higher refrigerating effect.
  5. Cylinder sizes can suit the volume of refrigerant; less leakage loss.
  6. More uniform torque, smaller flywheel; handles load variation.
Disadvantages
  1. Higher first cost: extra compressor, intercooler, flash chamber, controls.
  2. More complex piping and control, more maintenance.
  3. Not economical when the temperature lift is small.

Interstage pressure for equal pressure ratios: pi = √(pc pe)

Two-stage expansion with a flash cooler (2024 3a, 2023 2b)
  1. Dry saturated vapour at 1 enters the low-stage compressor and is compressed to interstage pressure pi (point 2).
  2. It mixes with flash vapour from the flash cooler (economizer); the mixture at 3 enters the high-stage compressor and leaves at pc (point 4).
  3. Condenser: desuperheated and condensed to liquid (point 5).
  4. First expansion valve (float valve) throttles 5→6 into the flash cooler. A part x flashes to vapour (7); its latent heat cools the remaining liquid to saturation at pi (8).
  5. Flash vapour (7) goes to the high-stage compressor; liquid (8) goes through the second expansion valve to 9 and into the evaporator.
  6. Evaporator: liquid evaporates to 1, completing the cycle.

Benefit: flash gas is not passed through the evaporator or low-stage compressor, the liquid entering the evaporator has lower enthalpy (more RE (refrigerating effect)), and the high-stage suction is cooler, so total work is less and COP (coefficient of performance) is higher.

Definitions you need first (2020 2b, 2021 2a)
  • Multistage compression: compressing the refrigerant from evaporator pressure to condenser pressure in two or more compressors (stages) in series, usually with intercooling / flash gas removal between stages, instead of one big pressure lift in one compressor.
  • Multipressure system: a refrigeration system that has two or more low-side (evaporator) pressures, for example one plant serving a freezer at −20 °C, a cold store at −5 °C and an air cooler at +5 °C, or a multistage system with an intermediate pressure.
Before you start: why several evaporators at different temperatures

Each load needs its own evaporator temperature. Running all of them at the lowest temperature would waste work, so each evaporator works at its own pressure pE1 < pE2 < pE3 (EP1 is the coldest).

Two ways to take the vapour back: one compressor (higher-pressure vapours are throttled down to pE1 by back-pressure valves), or one compressor per evaporator (no throttling of vapour).

(A) Single compressor with multiple expansion valves (2020 2b)

Working principle (write this):

  1. High-pressure liquid from the condenser (state 3) is throttled in E3 to pE3 (state 4). The flash vapour formed goes with the EP3 branch; only the liquid (5) continues.
  2. Liquid 5 is throttled in E2 to pE2 (state 7); again only the liquid (8) continues and is throttled in E1 to pE1 (state 10).
  3. Each evaporator EP3, EP2, EP1 absorbs its load Q3, Q2, Q1 and leaves as dry saturated vapour: 6, 9, 11.
  4. Back-pressure valves throttle vapour 6 and 9 down to the lowest pressure pE1 (6′, 9′; h does not change in throttling).
  5. All three vapours mix (state 1), are compressed isentropically in the one compressor to pc (state 2) and condensed (2→3).

Side note: Why expand in steps? The flash vapour made in E3 and E2 is removed early, so it does not travel through the colder evaporators where it would only take up space and give no cooling.

Derivation (masses in kg/min, Q in TR (ton of refrigeration (3.5 kW))):

Step (write this)Why / what it means
m1 = 210 Q1 / (h11 − h10),  h10 = h8Refrigerant needed by the coldest evaporator EP1: load ÷ refrigerating effect. Throttling: h10 = h8 (saturated liquid at pE2).
M2 = [210 Q2 + m1(h9 − h8)] / (h9 − h7),  h7 = h5Total flow through E2. Energy balance on the pE2 level: M2 enters at h7, m1 leaves as liquid h8, the rest leaves EP2 as vapour h9.
m2 = M2 − m1Vapour leaving the EP2 branch (refrigerating liquid + flash vapour from E2).
M3 = [210 Q3 + M2(h6 − h5)] / (h6 − h4),  h4 = h3Total flow through E3 = flow through the condenser and compressor. Same balance on the pE3 level.
m3 = M3 − M2Vapour leaving the EP3 branch.
h1 = (m1h11 + m2h9′ + m3h6′) / M3,  h9′ = h9, h6′ = h6Mixing of the three vapours before the compressor (mass-weighted average enthalpy). Find h2 from the chart along constant entropy from 1.
P = M3(h2 − h1) / 60 kWOne compressor handles the whole flow M3.
COP = 210(Q1 + Q2 + Q3) / [M3(h2 − h1)]Total cooling ÷ total work.

Side note: Units used in the course: Q in TR and 1 TR = 210 kJ/min, so 210Q is kJ/min and every mass flow m comes out in kg/min; divide by 60 to get kW. If Q is given in kW instead, drop the 210 and the 60: m = Q/Δh in kg/s and P = mΔh in kW.

Drawback: vapour from EP3 and EP2 is throttled down to pE1 and then compressed back up, so that pressure drop is wasted work; COP is lower than with individual compressors.

(B) Individual compressors with multiple expansion valves (2021 2a)

Working principle (write this):

  1. Liquid from the condenser (7) is throttled in E3 to pE3 (8). The flash vapour and the liquid needed by EP3 go to EP3; the remaining saturated liquid (8f) goes on.
  2. Liquid 8f is throttled in E2 to pE2 (9); EP2 takes its share, and the liquid 9f is throttled in E1 to pE1 (10) for EP1.
  3. EP3, EP2, EP1 absorb Q3, Q2, Q1 and deliver dry saturated vapour 5, 3, 1.
  4. Each vapour goes to its own compressor: C3 (5→6), C2 (3→4), C1 (1→2), all discharging at pc into the condenser. No back-pressure valves are needed.

Side note: Each compressor starts from its own evaporator pressure, so nothing is throttled down and pumped back up. That is why this system has a higher COP than (A).

Derivation (masses in kg/min, Q in TR):

Step (write this)Why / what it means
m1 = 210 Q1 / (h1 − h10),  h10 = h9fFlow through EP1 and compressor C1.
M2 = [210 Q2 + m1(h3 − h9f)] / (h3 − h9),  h9 = h8fTotal flow through valve E2 (energy balance on the pE2 level).
m2 = M2 − m1Flow through EP2 and compressor C2 (includes flash vapour from E2).
M3 = [210 Q3 + M2(h5 − h8f)] / (h5 − h8),  h8 = h7Total flow through E3 = flow through the condenser.
m3 = M3 − M2Flow through EP3 and compressor C3.
P = [m1(h2 − h1) + m2(h4 − h3) + m3(h6 − h5)] / 60 kWSum of the three compressor powers; h2, h4, h6 from the chart along constant entropy.
COP = 210(Q1 + Q2 + Q3) / [m1(h2 − h1) + m2(h4 − h3) + m3(h6 − h5)]Total cooling ÷ total work of the three compressors.

Side note: Units used in the course: Q in TR and 1 TR = 210 kJ/min, so 210Q is kJ/min and every mass flow m comes out in kg/min; divide by 60 to get kW. If Q is given in kW instead, drop the 210 and the 60: m = Q/Δh in kg/s and P = mΔh in kW.

Compare the two (one line each in the exam)
Single compressor + back-pressure valvesIndividual compressors
CompressorsOne, at the lowest suction pressure pE1One per evaporator, each at its own suction pressure
Back-pressure valvesNeeded on EP3 and EP2Not needed
Work / COPMore work (vapour throttled then recompressed), lower COPLess work, higher COP
CostCheap, simpleCostly: more compressors and controls
UseSmall plants, e.g. domestic / small cold storesLarge plants with very different temperature loads

Memory trick: Single = squeeze all the gas down to the coldest pressure, then pump once (wasteful). Individual = each gas pumped from where it is. In both, liquid flows E3 → E2 → E1, warm to cold, dropping its flash gas at each step.

Remember: >40 K lift → go multistage. Flash cooler = flash gas skips the evaporator and low stage. pi = √(pcpe).

A10 Performance of a practical plant: EER, SEER, kW/ton Likely · 70%Easy

Past-paper questions · Good to have

  • 2024 Q2(b) [8] How the full-load and part-load performance of a practical refrigeration plant measured? Briefly explain.
  • 2024 Q2(c) [15] Write notes on: (i) EER (energy efficiency ratio), (ii) SEER (seasonal energy efficiency ratio), (iii) kW/ton, (iv) Energy Star, (v) HSPF.
  • 2023 Q1(c) [8] How the performance of a practical refrigeration is evaluated? Describe.
Before you start: efficiency ratings

EER = cooling output in Btu/h per watt of electricity (EER = 3.412 × COP (coefficient of performance)). SEER = the same averaged over a cooling season. kW/ton = electric kW per TR (ton of refrigeration (3.5 kW)) of cooling (lower is better).

Measuring performance of a practical plant (2024 2b, 2023 1c)

COP of a real plant depends on outdoor conditions, components, application and season, so standard indices are used:

  • Full-load performance: COP, EER, or kW per ton at rated (100% load, standard test) conditions.
  • Part-load performance: SEER for small/unitary units; IPLV (integrated part-load value, at ARI standard conditions) and NPLV (non-standard) for chillers.

IPLV (or NPLV) = 0.01A + 0.42B + 0.45C + 0.12D

A, B, C, D = efficiency at 100% load (29.4 °C condenser water), 75% (23.9 °C), 50% (18.3 °C) and 25% (18.3 °C). The weights show that plants run mostly at 50-75% load.

Short notes (2024 2c)
IndexMeaningFormula / unit
EEREnergy efficiency ratio: cooling output per unit electrical input at one steady rated condition (outdoor 35 °C, indoor 27 °C)EER = Btu/h ÷ W; COP = EER/3.412
SEERSeasonal EER: total cooling over a whole season (Btu) ÷ total energy used (Wh); includes part-load running. US minimum 13 since 2006Btu/Wh
kW/tonElectrical input per ton of cooling; used for large chillers. Lower is better (good chillers 0.5-0.6)kW/ton = 12/EER = 3.517/COP
Energy StarUS EPA label for products with high efficiency (above minimum standards); helps buyers pick efficient units (e.g. split ≥ 14.5 SEER, 12 EER, 8.2 HSPF)Label
HSPFHeating seasonal performance factor: heat output over the heating season (Btu) ÷ electricity used (Wh), for air-source heat pumpsBtu/Wh

Remember: Full load: COP, EER, kW/ton. Part load: SEER, IPLV = 0.01A + 0.42B + 0.45C + 0.12D. kW/ton = 12/EER.

A15 Cooling towers and condensers Likely · 70%Easy

Past-paper questions · Skip if short

  • 2024 Q4(d) [6] Write down the classifications of cooling towers.
  • 2023 Q8(c) [9] Write down the classifications of cooling towers? Also describe how the performance of cooling tower is evaluated? (Section B)
  • 2023 Q4(c) [5] Write down the differences between air cooled condenser and water cooled condenser.
Before you start: rejecting heat

All heat removed plus compressor work must be rejected in the condenser: air-cooled (fins + fan), water-cooled (shell and tube, with a cooling tower to cool the water) or evaporative. A cooling tower cools water by evaporating a small part of it into air.

Not covered in the uploaded slides; written from standard textbooks (Arora, Khurmi). Check against class notes.

Classification of cooling towers (2024 4d, 2023 8c)
  • By draft: natural draft (atmospheric spray, hyperbolic chimney) and mechanical draft (forced draft: fan at inlet pushes air; induced draft: fan at top pulls air).
  • By air-water flow: counter-flow (air up, water down) and cross-flow (air horizontal).
  • By construction: open (wet) and closed-circuit (dry/fluid coolers); field-erected and factory-assembled.
Performance of a cooling tower

Range = Tw,in − Tw,out;   Approach = Tw,out − Twb,air;   Effectiveness = Range/(Range + Approach)

Also: cooling capacity = mwcp × range; L/G (water/air) ratio; evaporation loss ≈ 0.00085 × mw × range (°F) or about 1% per 6 K; drift and blowdown; cycles of concentration.

Air-cooled vs water-cooled condenser (2023 4c)
Air-cooledWater-cooled
Rejects heat to air by fansRejects heat to water (cooling tower loop)
Higher condensing temperature, lower COP (coefficient of performance)Lower condensing temperature, higher COP
No water needed, simple, low maintenanceNeeds water, tower, pumps, water treatment
Small/medium units (<~100 TR (ton of refrigeration (3.5 kW)))Large plants
Bigger, noisy fans, outdoor placementCompact condenser; scaling and fouling problems

Remember: Range = in − out. Approach = out − WBT (wet bulb temperature). Effectiveness = R/(R + A).

A12 Air refrigeration and aircraft cooling Likely · 60%Medium

Past-paper questions · Good to have

  • 2023 Q4(a) [10] Describe the working principle of an air refrigerator system. Also mention the necessity of cooling for an aircraft.
  • 2021 Q3(a) [10] What are the different methods of air refrigeration systems? Explain the simple air cooling system with necessary diagrams.
  • 2020 Q3(c) [13] In aircraft refrigeration unit using air cycle, 50 kg/min of air at 200 cm Hg gauge and 205 °C are bled off the air compressor serving the jet engine. The bled air passes through a heat exchanger leaving at 180 cm Hg gauge and 80 °C. It is then expanded through a small cooling turbine to 20 cm Hg vacuum and −10 °C. The air exhausted out of the plane is at 25 °C. Assume cp = 1.0 kJ/kgK. Determine the cooling capacity in TR (ton of refrigeration (3.5 kW)), and COP (coefficient of performance) based on input power to bled-off air.
Before you start: air refrigeration

Air itself can be the refrigerant: compress it, cool it at high pressure, then expand it in a turbine so it becomes very cold (reversed Brayton cycle). COP is low, but air is free, light and safe, so it is used in aircraft cabins.

Not covered in the uploaded slides; written from standard textbooks (Arora, Khurmi). Check against class notes.

Methods of air refrigeration (2021 3a)
  1. Simple air cooling system
  2. Simple evaporative system
  3. Boot-strap system
  4. Boot-strap evaporative system
  5. Reduced ambient system
  6. Regenerative air cooling system
Air refrigerator (Bell-Coleman / reversed Brayton) working principle (2023 4a)

Air is the refrigerant and stays a gas. Air from the cold room is compressed isentropically (1-2), cooled at constant pressure in a heat exchanger by cooling water (2-3), expanded isentropically in an expander/turbine to a very low temperature (3-4), and then absorbs heat from the cold room at constant pressure (4-1).

COP = (T1 − T4)/[(T2 − T3) − (T1 − T4)] = 1/(rp(γ−1)/γ − 1)

Simple air cooling system for aircraft

Ram air is compressed by the engine compressor; part is bled off, cooled in a heat exchanger by ram air, expanded in a cooling turbine to low temperature and supplied to the cabin. The turbine drives the cooling fan of the heat exchanger.

Why aircraft need cooling
  • Heat from passengers, avionics and equipment, solar radiation through the fuselage.
  • Ram (kinetic) heating of the skin at high speed; air from the compressor is very hot.
  • Cabin must be pressurized and ventilated with fresh air; outside air at altitude is thin.
  • Air cycle is chosen because it is light, uses no toxic refrigerant, and air is free and also gives pressurization.
Numerical (2020 3c)

m = 50 kg/min, cp = 1.0; turbine exit −10 °C; cabin exhaust 25 °C; bleed 205 °C.

Refrigerating effect = m cp(Tcabin − Tturbine exit) = 50 × 1.0 × (25 − (−10)) = 1750 kJ/min

Capacity = 1750/210 = 8.33 TR

Input energy carried by bled air (relative to the exhaust state) = m cp(205 − 25) = 50 × 180 = 9000 kJ/min

COP = 1750/9000 = 0.19

The paper does not say what "input power to bled-off air" is measured from; taking the cabin exhaust state (25 °C) as reference is the usual textbook choice. State it in the answer.

Remember: Air cycle: compress, cool, expand in turbine, absorb. Aircraft TR = m cp(Tcabin − Tturbine)/210.

A9 LiBr-water practical problems (crystallisation) Likely · 60%Medium

Past-paper questions · Good to have

  • 2024 Q4(a) [8] Briefly explain the various practical problems in water-lithium bromide vapor absorption refrigeration (VAR) system.
  • 2021 Q4(c) [7] What are the practical problems in LiBr-water vapor absorption system? Write a short note on crystallization problem.
Before you start: crystallisation

Lithium bromide solution is like very salty water. If it becomes too strong or too cold, salt crystals form and block the pipes (like sugar syrup crystallising). Plants avoid this with controls on concentration and temperature.

Not covered in the uploaded slides; written from standard textbooks (Arora, Khurmi). Check against class notes.

Practical problems in LiBr-water systems (2024 4a, 2021 4c)
  1. Crystallization: if the strong solution gets too concentrated or too cold (e.g. in the solution heat exchanger at low load, low cooling-water temperature, or power failure), LiBr (lithium bromide) salt crystallizes and blocks the pipes. Prevented by limiting concentration (<65%), controlling cooling water temperature, dilution cycle at shutdown, and an anti-crystallization (bypass) pipe.
  2. Very low (vacuum) pressure: water refrigerant runs at about 0.9 kPa in the evaporator, so air leaks in; purge units are needed to remove non-condensables, which otherwise cut capacity.
  3. Freezing of water: cannot be used below about 4 °C evaporator temperature since water freezes at 0 °C.
  4. Corrosion: LiBr is corrosive to steel and copper with oxygen present; inhibitors (lithium chromate, molybdate) are added.
  5. Large specific volume of water vapour: needs large vessels and pipes; pressure drop must be tiny, so components are housed in one or two shells.
  6. Hydrostatic head: even small liquid heights change the boiling pressure, so sprays and falling films are used.

Crystallization note: crystallization happens when the solution's state crosses the crystallization line on the Dühring/PTX chart. It is most likely at the hot-side outlet of the solution heat exchanger where the strong solution is coldest.

Remember: LiBr problems: Crystallization, Air leak (vacuum), Corrosion, Freezing (CACF).

A4 R22 VCR cycle numerical (with table / p-h chart) Likely · 70%Hard

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2024 Q1(c) [13] A refrigeration system using R22 is to have a refrigerating capacity of 80 kW. The system follows VCR (vapour compression refrigeration) cycle with 5 °C subcooling and 10 °C superheating in which the evaporating and condensing temperature are −10 °C and 45 °C, respectively. Determine: (i) the volume flow rate of refrigerant, (ii) COP (coefficient of performance), (iii) the power required to drive the compressor.
  • 2021 Q1(c) [15] Same question as 2024 1(c): R22, 80 kW, 5 °C subcooling, 10 °C superheating, evaporating −10 °C, condensing 45 °C. Find volume flow rate, COP and compressor power.
  • 2020 Q2(c) [12] A standard VCR system developing 50 kW of refrigeration using R22 refrigerant operates with a condensing temperature of 35 °C and an evaporating temperature of −10 °C. The enthalpy of the refrigerant after the compression is 435.2 kJ/kg. Using the table, determine: (i) the refrigeration effect in kJ/kg; (ii) the circulation rate of refrigerant in kg/s; (iii) the power required by the compressor in kW; and (iv) COP.
Before you start: reading refrigerant tables

State 1 = vapour leaving the evaporator (to compressor); 2 = hot vapour leaving the compressor; 3 = liquid leaving the condenser; 4 = after the expansion valve (h4 = h3 because throttling does no work and loses no heat).

Superheat = vapour heated above its boiling temperature; subcooling = liquid cooled below its condensing temperature. Isentropic compression means s2 = s1 (read h2 from the chart along the constant-entropy line).

Problem (2024 1c and 2021 1c): R22, 80 kW, te = −10 °C, tc = 45 °C, 5 K subcooling, 10 K superheat

Property values below are R22 table / p-h chart values (IIR reference, h = 200 kJ/kg at 0 °C liquid). Readings from your chart may differ by 1-2%; the method is what earns the marks.

Step 1: state points

pe = 3.55 bar (sat. at −10 °C); pc = 17.29 bar (sat. at 45 °C)

State 1: superheated vapour at 3.55 bar, −10 + 10 = 0 °C: h1 = 408.2 kJ/kg, s1 = 1.792 kJ/kg K, v1 = 0.0686 m³/kg

State 2: isentropic to 17.29 bar (s2 = s1): h2 = 450.4 kJ/kg (t2 ≈ 81 °C)

State 3: liquid at 45 − 5 = 40 °C: h3 = hf(40 °C) = 249.6 kJ/kg; h4 = h3 = 249.6 kJ/kg

Step 2: per kg

RE (refrigerating effect) = h1 − h4 = 408.2 − 249.6 = 158.6 kJ/kg

w = h2 − h1 = 450.4 − 408.2 = 42.2 kJ/kg

Step 3: mass flow m = 80 / 158.6 = 0.5045 kg/s

(i) Volume flow at suction V = m v1 = 0.5045 × 0.0686 = 0.0346 m³/s (2.08 m³/min)

(ii) COP = 158.6 / 42.2 = 3.75

(iii) Power = m w = 0.5045 × 42.2 = 21.3 kW

On the p-h sketch show: the horizontal evaporator line at 3.55 bar extending past the saturated vapour line to 1 (superheat), the isentropic line 1→2, the condenser line at 17.29 bar ending left of the saturated liquid line at 3 (subcooled), and the vertical throttling line 3→4. Use Fig 6.7 under A1 as the template.

Problem (2020 2c): R22, 50 kW, tc = 35 °C, te = −10 °C, h2 = 435.2 kJ/kg

−10 °C lies midway between −12 and −8: h1 = hg = (400.27 + 401.85)/2 = 401.06 kJ/kg

35 °C lies midway between 34 and 36: h3 = hf = (241.84 + 244.44)/2 = 243.14 kJ/kg = h4

(i) RE = 401.06 − 243.14 = 157.92 kJ/kg

(ii) m = 50 / 157.92 = 0.3166 kg/s

(iii) P = m (h2 − h1) = 0.3166 × (435.2 − 401.06) = 0.3166 × 34.14 = 10.81 kW

(iv) COP = 157.92 / 34.14 = 4.63

Remember: Find h1, h2, h3 (= h4) and v1 first. Then m = Q/RE, V = m v1, P = m w, COP = RE/w.

Same answer, step by step with reasons
Step (write this)Why / what it means
Read pe = 3.55 bar at −10 °C, pc = 17.29 bar at 45 °CSaturation pressures from the R22 table.
h1 = 408.2 kJ/kg (vapour at 0 °C = −10 + 10 superheat), v1 = 0.0686 m3/kgCompressor suction state.
h2 = 450.4 kJ/kg (follow constant s from 1 to 17.29 bar)Isentropic compression.
h3 = h4 = 249.6 kJ/kg (liquid at 40 °C = 45 − 5 subcool)Throttling keeps h constant.
RE = h1 − h4 = 158.6 kJ/kg; w = h2 − h1 = 42.2 kJ/kgCooling per kg and work per kg.
m = 80/158.6 = 0.5045 kg/sTotal cooling / cooling per kg.
V = m v1 = 0.0346 m3/s; COP = 158.6/42.2 = 3.75; P = m w = 21.3 kWVolume flow, COP, power.

Memory trick: "h1, h2, h3 then m": RE = h1 − h3, w = h2 − h1, m = Q/RE.

A14 Thermostatic expansion valve Possible · 50%Easy

Past-paper questions · Good to have

  • 2023 Q4(b) [10] Explain the thermostatic expansion valve with a neat sketch.
  • 2021 Q4(a) [12] What is the function of expansion valve in a refrigeration system? Explain the working principle of thermostatic expansion valve.
Before you start: expansion valve

The expansion valve controls how much refrigerant enters the evaporator. A thermostatic expansion valve (TEV) senses the superheat at the evaporator outlet with a bulb: too much superheat (evaporator starving) → opens more; too little → closes, so liquid never reaches the compressor.

Not covered in the uploaded slides; written from standard textbooks (Arora, Khurmi). Check against class notes.

Function of an expansion valve
  1. Reduce the pressure of liquid refrigerant from condenser pressure to evaporator pressure (throttling).
  2. Control the flow of refrigerant into the evaporator to match the load.
Thermostatic expansion valve (TEV)
  • Parts: valve body and needle, diaphragm, adjustable spring, feeler bulb clamped to the evaporator outlet, capillary tube joining bulb to the top of the diaphragm.
  • Forces: bulb pressure pb (top of diaphragm) opens the valve; evaporator pressure pe + spring pressure ps (below) close it. At balance pb = pe + ps.
  • It keeps a constant degree of superheat (about 5 K) at the evaporator outlet. When load rises, the vapour leaving gets more superheated, the bulb gets warmer, pb rises, the valve opens and more refrigerant flows. When load falls the opposite happens.
  • So the evaporator is kept well fed and no liquid reaches the compressor. Used in most DX systems.

Sketch: draw the valve with diaphragm at top, spring below, needle in the liquid line, capillary to a bulb on the suction line after the evaporator.

Remember: TEV (thermostatic expansion valve): bulb pressure opens; evaporator + spring close. Keeps superheat constant.

A16 Linde air liquefaction Possible · 20%Medium

Past-paper questions · Skip if short

  • 2021 Q3(c) [10] Describe the Linde system of liquefaction of air.
Before you start: liquefying air

The Linde process: compress air, cool it, then expand it through a throttle valve; real gases cool on throttling (Joule-Thomson effect). A counter-flow heat exchanger pre-cools the incoming air with the cold returning gas, until part of it becomes liquid.

Not covered in the uploaded slides; written from standard textbooks (Arora, Khurmi). Check against class notes.

Linde system of air liquefaction (2021 3c)
  1. Atmospheric air is compressed to about 200 bar in a multistage compressor with intercooling, then cooled to ambient in an after-cooler (nearly isothermal compression).
  2. High-pressure air passes through a counter-flow heat exchanger where it is cooled by the cold unliquefied air returning from the separator.
  3. It is then throttled through an expansion valve (Joule-Thomson effect); the temperature drops further and a fraction y of air liquefies.
  4. Liquid is collected in a separator; the cold vapour returns through the heat exchanger (pre-cooling the incoming air) and is mixed with make-up air at the compressor inlet.

Yield y = (h1 − h2)/(h1 − hf)  (1 = low-pressure gas at ambient, 2 = high-pressure gas at ambient, f = saturated liquid)

Throttling cools only because air is below its inversion temperature. The process starts slowly and becomes continuous once the heat exchanger has cooled down.

Remember: Linde: compress, cool, regenerate in HX, throttle (J-T), separate liquid.

A11 Ammonia ice-plant numerical (COP % of theoretical) Possible · 50%Hard

Past-paper questions · Good to have

  • 2023 Q2(c) [12] An ammonia refrigerator produces 25 tonnes of ice from and at 0 °C in 24 hours. The temperature range of the compressor is from 15 °C to −5 °C. The vapor is dry saturated at the end of compression and an expansion valve is used. Assume a COP (coefficient of performance) of 45% of the theoretical value. Calculate the power required to drive the compressor. Latent heat of ice is 335 kJ/kg.
  • 2021 Q2(c) [15] Same as above with 30 tonnes of ice, compressor range 20 °C to −10 °C, COP = 55% of theoretical.
Before you start: ice plant numerical idea

Find the cooling load (kW) from the ice made per day. Find the theoretical COP from ammonia table values (dry saturated after compression means state 2 is on the vapour line, so s1 = s2 = sg at condenser temperature). Actual COP = given % × theoretical. Power = load / actual COP.

Dryness fraction x = fraction of vapour in a wet mixture: s = sf + x(sg − sf), h = hf + x(hg − hf).

Method (from the slides' worked example, 30 t ice, 25 °C to −15 °C, COP 60%: answer 33.2 kW)
  1. Load: 1 tonne of ice per day from and at 0 °C = 1000 × 335/86400 = 3.88 kW.
  2. Dry saturated at the end of compression: s1 = s2 = sg at condenser temperature. Find x1 from s1 = sf1 + x1(sg1 − sf1), then h1 = hf1 + x1(hg1 − hf1).
  3. COPth = (h1 − hf3)/(h2 − h1); COPactual = % × COPth; P = Q/COPactual.
2023 2(c): 25 t ice/day, 15 °C to −5 °C, COP = 45% of theoretical

NH3 table (same reference as the slides): at 15 °C hf = 251.4, hg = 1457.5 kJ/kg, sg = 5.1493; at −5 °C hf = 158.4, hg = 1437.6 kJ/kg, sf = 0.6313, sg = 5.4019 kJ/kg K

x1 = (5.1493 − 0.6313)/(5.4019 − 0.6313) = 0.947

h1 = 158.4 + 0.947(1437.6 − 158.4) = 1369.9 kJ/kg

COPth = (1369.9 − 251.4)/(1457.5 − 1369.9) = 1118.5/87.6 = 12.77

COPactual = 0.45 × 12.77 = 5.75

Q = 25 × 1000 × 335/86400 = 96.9 kW

Power = 96.9/5.75 = 16.9 kW

2021 2(c): 30 t ice/day, 20 °C to −10 °C, COP = 55% of theoretical

At 20 °C hf = 275.0, hg = 1461.3, sg = 5.0910; at −10 °C hf = 135.5, hg = 1431.7, sf = 0.5454, sg = 5.4712

x1 = (5.0910 − 0.5454)/(5.4712 − 0.5454) = 0.923; h1 = 135.5 + 0.923(1296.2) = 1331.7 kJ/kg

COPth = (1331.7 − 275.0)/(1461.3 − 1331.7) = 1056.7/129.6 = 8.15; actual = 0.55 × 8.15 = 4.48

Q = 30 × 3.877 = 116.3 kW

Power = 116.3/4.48 = 26.0 kW

Use the NH3 table given in the exam; values above may differ by a few kJ/kg but the COP will be very close.

Remember: Ice tonnes × 3.88 kW. x1 from entropy, h1 from x1, then COP × %.

Same answer, step by step with reasons
Step (write this)Why / what it means
Q = 25 t/day × 1000 × 335 / 86,400 = 96.9 kWIce made per second × latent heat. 86,400 s per day.
x1 = (sg at 15 °C − sf at −5 °C)/(sfg at −5 °C) = 0.947Entropy same before and after compression; state 2 is dry saturated at 15 °C.
h1 = 158.4 + 0.947 × 1279.2 = 1369.9 kJ/kgEnthalpy of the wet vapour entering the compressor.
COPth = (1369.9 − 251.4)/(1457.5 − 1369.9) = 12.77(h1 − hf3) / (h2 − h1).
COPactual = 0.45 × 12.77 = 5.75; Power = 96.9/5.75 = 16.9 kWReal machine reaches only 45 % of ideal.
