Section B: Air conditioning

Sort Section B:

B1 Psychrometric definitions Very likely · 100%Easy

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2024 Q5(a) [12] Define: (i) Humid specific heat, (ii) Sensible heat factor, (iii) Degree of saturation, (iv) Bypass factor.
  • 2023 Q5(a) [12] Define: (i) Specific humidity, (ii) Degree of saturation, (iii) Wet bulb temperature, (iv) Humid specific heat.
  • 2023 Q5(b) [6] What is meant by SHF? How SHF line is drawn in psychrometric chart?
  • 2021 Q5(a) [12] Define: (i) Dew point temperature, (ii) Relative humidity, (iii) Wet bulb temperature, (iv) Sensible heat factor.
  • 2020 Q4(a) [10] What is meant by bypass factor? How do you draw sensible heat factor (SHF) line on a psychrometric chart?
Before you start: psychrometry in one minute

Psychrometry = study of moist air (dry air + water vapour). Dry bulb temperature (DBT) = normal thermometer reading. Wet bulb (WBT) = reading with a wet wick (lower, because water evaporates). Dew point (DPT) = temperature at which water starts to condense. Specific humidity ω = kg water per kg dry air. Relative humidity (RH) = how close the air is to saturation (%).

The psychrometric chart plots all of these; you find a point from any two values.

Each term carries 3 marks. Write the definition, the formula, and one line on why it matters.

TermDefinitionFormula
Dry bulb temp (DBT)Temperature of moist air read by an ordinary thermometer.–
Wet bulb temp (WBT)Lowest temperature reached by evaporating water into the air, read by a thermometer whose bulb has a wet wick in moving air. DBT (dry bulb temperature) − WBT (wet bulb temperature) = wet bulb depression; larger depression means drier air. Saturated air: WBT = DBT.DPT (dew point temperature) ≤ WBT ≤ DBT
Dew point temp (DPT)Temperature at which moisture starts to condense when unsaturated air is cooled at constant pressure (constant w). Saturated air: DPT = DBT.psat(DPT) = pv
Specific humidity / humidity ratio (w)Mass of water vapour per kg of dry air. Does not change with temperature unless moisture is added or removed.w = 0.622 pv/(pt − pv) kg/kg d.a.
Relative humidity (φ)Ratio of the vapour partial pressure to the saturation pressure at the same DBT; shows how close air is to saturation. Strongly depends on temperature.φ = pv/psat
Degree of saturation (μ)Ratio of the humidity ratio to the humidity ratio of saturated air at the same temperature and pressure. 0 for dry air, 1 for saturated air; nearly equal to φ.μ = w/ws = φ(pt − ps)/(pt − pv)
Humid specific heat (cpm)Heat needed to raise 1 kg of dry air plus its water vapour by 1 K.cpm = 1.005 + 1.88w ≈ 1.0216 kJ/kg K
Enthalpy (h)Enthalpy of dry air + enthalpy of its vapour per kg dry air.h = 1.005t + w(2501 + 1.88t) kJ/kg d.a.
Sensible heat factor (SHF)Ratio of sensible heat to total heat of a process. 1 = pure sensible, 0 = pure latent; 0.75-0.80 normal, ~0.6 in humid climates.SHF = Qs/(Qs + QL)
Bypass factor (X)Fraction of air passing the coil that does not touch it and leaves at inlet state; exit air is a mix, so it never reaches ADP (apparatus dew point). Contact factor = 1 − X. Lowered by more coil rows, lower air velocity, closer fins.X = (tc − ts)/(to − ts)
Apparatus dew point (ADP)Effective coil surface temperature; where the condition (SHF) line meets the saturation curve.ts = tADP
Bypass factor on the chart
How to draw the SHF line on the psychrometric chart (2023 5b, 2020 4a)
  1. You need two things: the initial state (room point) and the SHF.
  2. On the chart's protractor (SHF scale), join the reference point (26 °C, 50% RH (relative humidity)) to the given SHF value.
  3. Draw a line parallel to it through the room state point. That line is the SHF line; extend it to meet the saturation curve at the ADP.

tan θ = Δw/ΔT = (1/2451)(1 − SHF)/SHF   (slope depends only on SHF)

Psychrometry is the study of the properties of moist air (mixture of dry air and water vapour) and the processes that change them.

Remember: Three temperatures: DBT ≥ WBT ≥ DPT (all equal when saturated). w = 0.622 pv/(pt − pv). SHF = Qs/Qt. X = (tc − ts)/(to − ts).

B4 Thermal comfort and the ASHRAE comfort chart Very likely · 100%Easy

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2024 Q6(a) [5] Draw the ASHRAE (American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers) comfort chart.
  • 2024 Q6(b) [5] Is it impossible to satisfy a thermal environment that satisfies everyone? Explain with the equation: PPD = 100 − 95 × e−0.03353 PMV4 − 0.2179 PMV2
  • 2023 Q6(a) [5] Draw the ASHRAE comfort chart.
  • 2023 Q6(b) [6] What is meant by indoor design conditions and outdoor design conditions?
  • 2021 Q6(a) [8] What is meant by thermal comfort? What are the factors affecting thermal comfort?
  • 2020 Q4(b) [10] What is meant by thermal comfort? What are the factors affecting thermal comfort?
  • 2020 Q4(c) [6] Distinguish between effective temperature and operative temperature.
  • 2020 Q4(d) [4] Draw the ASHRAE comfort chart.
Before you start: comfort

People feel comfortable around 23-26 °C with 40-60 % RH (relative humidity) and gentle air movement. The effective temperature combines temperature, humidity and air speed into one number; the ASHRAE comfort chart shows the comfort zone on psychrometric axes.

Thermal comfort and its factors (2021 6a, 2020 4b)

Thermal comfort is the condition of mind which expresses satisfaction with the thermal environment (ASHRAE 55). The body is comfortable when its heat production equals its heat loss without strain.

  1. Environmental: air (dry bulb) temperature, mean radiant temperature (MRT), relative humidity, air velocity.
  2. Personal: activity level (metabolic rate, met) and clothing insulation (clo).
  3. Others: age, sex, health, acclimatization, air purity.
ASHRAE comfort chart (5 marks, asked 3 times)
  • Drawn on psychrometric axes: operative temperature on x, humidity ratio on y.
  • Comfort zones are bounded by effective temperature (ET) lines, the 60% RH line on top and 2 °C dew point at the bottom.
  • Winter zone: ET 20 to 23.5 °C. Summer zone: ET 22.5 to 26 °C. In the overlap, people in winter clothes feel slightly warm and in summer clothes slightly cool.
  • Humidity limits avoid dry skin, eye irritation, respiratory problems and microbial growth.
Effective vs operative temperature (2020 4c)
Effective temperature (ET)Operative temperature (to)
Temperature of a standard environment at 50% RH that gives the same heat loss from the skin (same feeling) as the actual environmentUniform temperature of an imaginary black enclosure in which a person exchanges the same heat by radiation + convection as in the actual space
Combines air temp, humidity (and air motion)Combines air temp and mean radiant temp; humidity not included
Lines of constant ET bound the comfort zonesto ≈ (ta + tmrt)/2 at low air speed; x-axis of comfort chart
PMV-PPD (2024 6b): can everyone be satisfied?

PPD = 100 − 95 exp(−0.03353 PMV4 − 0.2179 PMV2)

PMV (predicted mean vote) is the average vote on the 7-point scale (−3 cold … 0 neutral … +3 hot). PPD is the % of people dissatisfied. Put the best case PMV = 0: PPD = 100 − 95 e0 = 5%. So even in the ideal environment at least 5% of people are still dissatisfied, because people differ in clothing, activity and preference. It is impossible to satisfy everyone; ASHRAE aims for PPD < 10% (−0.5 < PMV < +0.5).

Indoor and outdoor design conditions (2023 6b)
  • Indoor design conditions: the DBT (dry bulb temperature), RH and air velocity to be maintained inside for comfort or process, chosen from the comfort chart. Typical summer comfort: 24-26 °C DBT, 50-60% RH, 0.15-0.25 m/s air speed; winter: 20-22 °C.
  • Outdoor design conditions: the DBT and WBT (and daily range) of the location used for sizing equipment, taken from long-term weather data (e.g. 1%, 2.5% values that are exceeded only that fraction of hours). Not the absolute worst day, to avoid oversizing. Example: Dhaka summer ≈ 36 °C DBT / 28 °C WBT (wet bulb temperature).

Remember: Comfort chart: ET lines + 60% RH top + 2 °C DPT (dew point temperature) bottom; summer 22.5-26, winter 20-23.5. PMV 0 still gives PPD 5%.

B5 Indoor air quality (IAQ) and ventilation Very likely · 100%Easy

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2024 Q6(c) [15] Dhaka has twice the CO2 concentration of Khulna (400 ppm). If a class room with 30 students is in a room of same size in both cities, determine the required ventilation rate for each location. Also, explain how to control IAQ (indoor air quality) in a classroom.
  • 2023 Q6(d) [12] What are effects of IAQ on health and comfort? How to control IAQ?
  • 2021 Q6(d) [10] Write short notes on: (i) Filtration, and (ii) Dilution.
  • 2020 Q5(c) [6] What are the effects of indoor air quality on health and comfort? How to control indoor air quality?
Before you start: fresh air

Indoor air gets stale (CO2 from breathing, odours, VOCs). Ventilation brings in outside air to dilute it, typically 7.5-10 L/s per person, keeping CO2 below about 1000 ppm.

IAQ and its effects on health and comfort (2023 6d, 2020 5c)

Indoor air quality (IAQ) is the condition of air inside buildings as it affects the health, comfort and well-being of occupants. People spend about 90% of time indoors, and indoor air can be 2-5 times more polluted than outdoor air (US EPA).

  • Sick building syndrome (SBS): acute discomfort linked to time in a building, with no specific cause found; symptoms improve when the person leaves. Symptoms: cough, chest tightness, eye/nose/throat irritation, dry or itchy skin, headache, dizziness, nausea, fatigue, poor concentration.
  • Building-related illness (BRI): medically identifiable disease that persists after leaving: allergic (asthma, rhinitis, hypersensitivity pneumonitis from mold, dust, VOCs), infections (Legionnaires' disease, TB, COVID-19), skin diseases (eczema, dermatitis).
  • Pollutants: CO2 and odours from people, VOCs from paints and furniture, particulates, mold spores, bacteria, CO/NOx from combustion, radon.
How to control IAQ: three methods
  1. Source control (most effective): low-VOC paints and furniture, no smoking, local exhaust; place outdoor intakes 8-10 ft above ground, away from loading docks and 10-15 ft from exhaust outlets; keep RH (relative humidity) below 60% to stop mold.
  2. Filtration: remove particles 0.1-200 μm. Efficiency = (Cup − Cdown)/Cup × 100. Filter types by MERV: panel (1-4), pleated (5-8), bag/pocket (9-15), HEPA (99.97% at 0.3 μm), ULPA (99.999% at 0.12 μm). Selection: cleanliness needed, dust type, pressure drop, space, cost, dust disposal.
  3. Dilution (ventilation): bring in filtered outdoor air to dilute CO2 and contaminants. By natural ventilation, forced (fan) ventilation, or infiltration (uncontrolled leakage). A CO2 sensor can set the outdoor-air damper (demand-controlled ventilation).

Short notes (2021 6d): Filtration = removing particles and gases from supply air with filters (see list above); Dilution = lowering pollutant concentration by mixing in clean outdoor air (ventilation).

Numerical (2024 6c): classroom of 30 students, Khulna 400 ppm, Dhaka 800 ppm

CO2 balance: V · Cout + N = V · Cspace → V = n Np / (Cspace − Cout)

Take Np = 0.011 cfm CO2 per person (1.2 met, seated students) and allowable indoor Cspace = 1000 ppm (class 09 values).

Khulna: V = 30 × 0.011 / [(1000 − 400) × 10−6] = 0.33/0.0006 = 550 cfm (18.3 cfm/person) = 550 × 0.4719 = 260 L/s ≈ 0.26 m³/s

Dhaka (Cout = 800 ppm): V = 0.33 / [(1000 − 800) × 10−6] = 1650 cfm (55 cfm/person) = 779 L/s ≈ 0.78 m³/s

Dhaka needs 3 times the fresh air of Khulna, because the cleaner-air margin (1000 − Cout) is only 200 ppm instead of 600 ppm.

Controlling IAQ in the classroom: CO2-sensor-controlled fresh-air damper or exhaust fan; filter the fresh air (MERV 8-13, since Dhaka's outdoor air is dusty); keep RH 40-60%; low-VOC materials; open windows in breaks for cross-ventilation; regular cleaning and filter replacement.

Remember: Source control, Filtration, Dilution. V = nNp/(Cin − Cout).

B2 Psychrometric processes and the air washer Very likely · 90%Easy

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2024 Q5(b) [8] What is an air washer? Describe the following process with an air washer: (i) Cooling and Dehumidification, (ii) Heating and Humidification.
  • 2023 Q5(c) [6] Explain the working principle of an air washer.
  • 2021 Q5(b) [8] What is psychrometry? Describe the following process in a psychrometric chart: (i) Cooling and dehumidification, (ii) Heating and humidification.
Before you start: processes on the chart

Heating/cooling only = horizontal line (ω constant). Cooling below dew point = dehumidification (moves left and down). Adding steam/water spray = humidification (moves up). Mixing two air streams = point on the straight line between them, closer to the bigger stream. An air washer sprays water into air.

Basic processes on the chart
(i) Cooling and dehumidification
  • Air is passed over a coil whose surface temperature is below the air's DPT (dew point temperature). Vapour condenses, so both DBT (dry bulb temperature) and w fall (process O→C, down and to the left).
  • Water removed: mw = ma(wo − wc). Coil load: Qt = ma(ho − hc).
  • Qs = macpm(to − tc), QL = mahfg(wo − wc). Used in summer AC.
(ii) Heating and humidification
  • Air is first sensibly heated by a heating coil, then water vapour (steam) or warm water spray is added. DBT and w both rise (up and to the right).
  • Q = ma(h2 − h1) − mwhw; used in winter AC for comfort.
Air washer (2024 5b, 2023 5c)

An air washer is a chamber in which air comes in direct contact with a spray of water; heat and moisture are exchanged between them. Eliminator plates stop water droplets leaving with the air; a pump recirculates the water through a cooler or heater; make-up water replaces evaporated water. The outlet air state is controlled by the water temperature tw. Heat flows down the temperature gradient and moisture flows down the vapour pressure gradient.

Water temperatureProcessWater must be
tw < DPTO-A Cooling and dehumidificationExternally cooled
tw = DPTSensible cooling (w constant)Cooled
DPT < tw < WBT (wet bulb temperature)O-C Cooling and humidificationCooled
tw = WBTO-B Adiabatic (evaporative) cooling, h constantJust recirculated
WBT < tw < DBTO-D Cooling and humidification, h risesExternally heated
tw > DBTO-E Heating and humidificationExternally heated

With an air washer: cooling and dehumidification is done by spraying chilled water below the air's DPT; heating and humidification is done by spraying hot water above the air's DBT. Humidifying efficiency ηH = (w2 − w1)/(ws − w1) = contact factor = 1 − X.

Remember: Air washer: the water temperature decides everything. Below DPT dries, at WBT is evaporative, above DBT heats.

B6 Air-conditioning systems: zone, all-air CAV / VAV, dual duct Very likely · 100%Medium

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2024 Q7(a) [8] What is meant by zone? Explain dual duct constant air volume air conditioning system with schematic diagram.
  • 2024 Q6(d) [10] Using the data given in the following table, make a system choice matrix and explain which system will be most appropriate for KUET academic building's thermal load.
  • 2023 Q6(c) [12] Describe the various all-air central air-conditioning system.
  • 2021 Q6(b) [9] What is meant by zone? Explain the difference between constant air volume and variable air volume air-conditioning system with schematic diagram.
  • 2021 Q6(c) [8] What are the advantages and disadvantages of rooftop air-conditioning unit?
  • 2020 Q5(a) [9] Classify air-conditioning system. Explain the working principle of split air-conditioning system with schematic diagram.
  • 2020 Q5(b) [7] Distinguish between constant air volume and variable air volume of all-air central air-conditioning system. What are the advantages of all-air systems?
Before you start: AC system types

All-air systems send cooled air through ducts from a central air handling unit (AHU). CAV (constant air volume) (constant air volume) varies supply temperature; VAV (variable air volume) (variable air volume) keeps temperature fixed and varies the amount of air to each zone with dampers (saves fan energy). Dual duct = one hot and one cold duct mixed at each room.

The uploaded Section B slides do not cover air distribution systems, so this answer is from standard textbooks (Arora, McQuiston, ASHRAE (American Society of Heating, Refrigerating and Air-Conditioning Engineers)). Check it against your class notes.

Zone

A zone is a space or group of spaces whose load pattern is similar enough to be controlled by one thermostat (one control point). Example: all west-facing offices form one zone; the interior core forms another.

Classification of AC systems (2020 5a)
  • By purpose: comfort AC, industrial AC
  • By season: summer, winter, year-round
  • By equipment arrangement: unitary (window, split, packaged/rooftop) and central
  • By medium to the room: all-air, all-water, air-water, refrigerant-based (DX, VRF (variable refrigerant flow))
Split AC working principle (2020 5a)

The indoor unit holds the evaporator coil, blower and filter; it cools and dehumidifies room air. The outdoor unit holds the compressor, condenser and fan, and rejects heat outside. Refrigerant flows between them in two copper pipes (liquid and suction). It follows the VCR (vapour compression refrigeration) cycle; quiet indoors because the compressor is outside; needs no ducts.

All-air central systems (2023 6c)

Air is the only medium that carries heating/cooling to the space; a central AHU (filter, coils, fan) conditions it and ducts deliver it.

  1. Single duct, constant air volume (CAV), single zone: constant flow, supply temperature varied (or reheat) by one thermostat.
  2. Single duct CAV with terminal reheat: air cooled to ~13 °C, reheated per zone; good control, wasteful.
  3. Multizone: hot and cold decks at the AHU (air handling unit) mixed per zone by dampers; one duct per zone.
  4. Dual duct (CAV or VAV): separate hot and cold ducts to mixing boxes at each zone.
  5. Variable air volume (VAV): constant supply temperature, VAV boxes vary the airflow to each zone.
Dual duct CAV system (2024 7a)

Return/fresh air is filtered and handled by one fan, then split into a hot duct (through a heating coil) and a cold duct (through a cooling coil). At each zone a mixing box with two linked dampers, worked by the zone thermostat, mixes hot and cold air in the right proportion. The total air to each zone stays constant; only its temperature changes. Advantages: each zone gets independent control at any time; heating and cooling available together. Disadvantages: two ducts take space and cost more; mixing hot and cold air wastes energy.

CAV vs VAV (2021 6b, 2020 5b)
Constant air volume (CAV)Variable air volume (VAV)
Airflow constant; supply temperature varies with loadSupply temperature constant; airflow varies with load
Simple, low first cost, steady ventilationVAV box per zone, variable-speed fan, more controls
Fan always at full power; reheat wastes energyFan power drops at part load; large energy saving
Suits single zone or uniform loadSuits multi-zone buildings with varying loads
Good air distribution at all loadsAt low flow, ventilation and air distribution can suffer (minimum box setting needed)

Advantages of all-air systems: central equipment away from occupied space (easy maintenance, no water or drains in rooms); good humidity control and filtration; can use free cooling with outdoor air (economizer); simultaneous heating and cooling in different zones; quiet rooms. Disadvantages: large ducts and shafts, more fan energy, needs ceiling space.

Rooftop unit: advantages and disadvantages (2021 6c)
AdvantagesDisadvantages
Self-contained, factory assembled and tested; quick to installRoof must carry the weight; roof penetration can leak
Saves indoor floor space and plant roomExposed to weather; shorter life
Noise and maintenance kept outside occupied areaService work on the roof is awkward
Easy to add economizer, lower first costLower efficiency than central chillers for large buildings; limited duct runs
System choice matrix (2024 6d)

Score = Σ (relative importance × performance)

Split: 8×8 + 9×8 + 10×7 + 5×6 + 9×6 + 8×7 = 64 + 72 + 70 + 30 + 54 + 56 = 346

Rooftop: 8×10 + 9×9 + 10×8 + 5×8 + 9×9 + 8×9 = 80 + 81 + 80 + 40 + 81 + 72 = 434

Rooftop unit scores higher (434 vs 346, out of 490) and is the better choice for the KUET academic building. It wins on cooling capacity, maintenance and energy, which matter for a large building with long operating hours.

Remember: CAV: fixed air, vary temperature. VAV: fixed temperature, vary air. Dual duct: hot + cold duct mixed per zone.

B9 Duct sizing numerical (equal friction method) Very likely · 100%Medium

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2024 Q8(c) [15] For the duct system as shown in figure, determine the dimension of rectangular duct with aspect ratio 3:1. Assume all dynamic loss coefficients are 0.8.
  • 2023 Q8(d) [15] Determine the size of the duct system shown in figure using equal friction method assuming pressure drop of 0.1 mm H2O/m length.
  • 2021 Q8(d) [14] For the duct system as shown in figure, determine the dimensions AB, BC, CD and DE of the rectangular ducts with aspect ratio 3:1 assuming friction rate of 0.1 mm H2O/m length duct.
  • 2020 Q6(c) [12] Determine the dimensions of AB, BC, CD as shown in figure using equal friction method. Choose a friction rate of 0.09 mm H2O/m. Use Δpf/L = 0.002268 × Q1.852/D4.973 mm H2O/m (Q in m³/s, D in m).
Before you start: duct sizing

Air needs a pressure push to flow through ducts; friction loses some pressure per metre. In the equal friction method every duct section is sized for the same friction loss per metre. Bigger flow → bigger diameter. For a rectangular duct use the equivalent diameter De = 1.3(ab)0.625/(a + b)0.25.

Duct design is not in the uploaded slides. The method below is the standard equal friction method (Arora ch. 22); the friction formula is the one printed on the 2020 paper. Rectangular sizes use the equivalent diameter De = 1.3(ab)0.625/(a + b)0.25.

Before you start: what a duct-sizing question is asking

Air leaves the fan and travels through one main duct that splits into branches, each ending at an outlet (a grille in a room). You are told how much air each outlet needs. You must pick a size for every piece of duct so the air gets there, and then find how much pressure the fan must give to push it through the longest path.

Bigger duct = slower air = less rubbing loss but more sheet metal. The equal friction method fixes the loss per metre (f) to the same value in every section, so every section is sized with one formula.

Symbols used in B9 (read this first)
SymbolWhat it isUnitPlain meaning
QVolume flow rate of airm³/sHow many cubic metres of air pass through that duct every second. Given at each outlet.
fFriction rate (pressure loss per metre)mm H2O per mHow much pressure the air loses by rubbing on the walls in each metre of straight duct. Given (0.09 or 0.1), same for every section.
DDiameter of a round ductmThe size you are solving for when the duct is round.
a, bLong side and short side of a rectangular ductmWidth and height of the box-shaped duct. "Aspect ratio 3:1" means a = 3b.
DeEquivalent diametermThe round-duct diameter that gives the same friction loss at the same Q as the rectangle a × b. It lets you use the round formula for a rectangular duct.
VAir velocitym/sHow fast the air moves: V = Q / area.
ACross-section area of the ductm²Round: πD²/4. Rectangle: a × b.
LLength of a duct sectionmRead from the layout drawing.
ρDensity of airkg/m³Take 1.2 kg/m³.
pvVelocity pressurePa or mm H2OThe pressure "carried" by the moving air, ρV²/2. Fittings lose a fraction K of it.
KDynamic loss coefficientno unitFraction of pv lost at a bend, junction or elbow (given 0.8 in 2024).
mm H2OMillimetre of water column1 mm H2O = 9.81 PaA small pressure unit used for fans and ducts.
Index runThe longest path from fan to the farthest outletThe fan must overcome the loss along this path, so the fan pressure is calculated on it.
0.002268, 1.852, 4.973Constants of the friction formulaFixed numbers from the duct friction chart (printed on the 2020 paper). Just copy them.
Each equation in plain words
EquationRead it asUse it to
Qsection = sum of the outlet Q downstreamA duct carries all the air that leaves after it.Get Q for every section. Start at the far outlets and add backwards to the fan.
f = 0.002268 Q1.852 / D4.973Loss per metre rises with more air (Q) and falls very fast with a bigger duct (D to the power about 5).Link flow, size and loss.
D = (0.002268 Q1.852 / f)1/4.973The same formula turned round to give the size. 1/4.973 ≈ 0.201.Find the round diameter. On a calculator: Q^1.852 × 0.002268 ÷ f, then ^0.201.
De = 1.3 (ab)0.625 / (a + b)0.25The round size that behaves like the rectangle a × b.Convert between rectangle and round. Here, set De = D from the line above.
a = 3b ⇒ b ≈ 0.548 D, a ≈ 1.643 DPutting a = 3b into the De formula gives De = 1.827 b, so b = D/1.827.Get the rectangle sides in one step (3:1 ducts only).
V = Q / ASpeed = flow ÷ area.Fill the velocity column and check it is sensible (about 5-10 m/s).
Friction loss = f × Lindex runLoss per metre × metres of the longest path.Get the straight-duct part of the fan pressure.
pv = ρV²/2 (Pa); in mm H2O = 1.2V²/(2 × 9.81)Divide Pa by 9.81 to get mm H2O.Get the velocity pressure at each fitting.
Dynamic loss = K × pvEach fitting wastes a fraction K of the velocity pressure.Add the losses at bends and junctions on the index run.
Fan pressure = friction loss + dynamic lossesTotal push the fan must give on the longest path.Final answer of the fan part.

Side note: Where does De = 1.827 b come from? With a = 3b: ab = 3b² and a + b = 4b. So De = 1.3 × 30.625 × b1.25 / (40.25 × b0.25) = 1.3 × 1.987 / 1.414 × b = 1.827 b. You can write this one line in the exam to justify the quick rule.

Equal friction method in 5 steps
  1. Write the airflow in each section by adding the outlet flows downstream of it.
  2. Choose a constant friction rate f (given: 0.09 or 0.1 mm H2O per m) for every section.
  3. Find the round diameter from the friction chart or formula: f = 0.002268 Q1.852/D4.973 ⇒ D = (0.002268 Q1.852/f)1/4.973
  4. For a rectangular duct with a = 3b, solve De = 1.3(3b²)0.625/(4b)0.25 for b. Quick rule: for 3:1, b ≈ 0.548 D, a ≈ 1.643 D.
  5. Fan total pressure = f × (length of the longest run) + dynamic losses (K × velocity pressure) on that run.

B7 VRF systems (two-pipe / three-pipe heat recovery) Very likely · 100%Medium

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2024 Q7(b) [12] What is meant by VRF (variable refrigerant flow) system? Explain three pipe heat recovery VRF systems with necessary sketches.
  • 2023 Q7(b) [7] Distinguish between multi-split system and VRF system.
  • 2021 Q7(a) [12] What is meant by VRF system? Explain three-pipe heat recovery VRF systems with required sketches.
  • 2021 Q7(b) [8] What are the differences between a heat pump multisplit system and a VRF multisplit system?
  • 2020 Q5(d) [8] What are the advantages of VRF system? Draw the block diagram of two-pipe heat recovery VRF system.
Before you start: VRF

Variable refrigerant flow: one outdoor unit with a variable-speed compressor feeds many indoor units by refrigerant pipes (no ducts, no chilled water). Two-pipe = all units cool or all heat; three-pipe heat recovery = some rooms can cool while others heat, moving heat between them.

VRF is not in the uploaded slides; this answer is from standard textbooks and manufacturer literature.

What is VRF

Variable refrigerant flow (VRF) is a ductless multi-split DX system in which one outdoor unit with an inverter (variable speed) compressor serves many indoor units through refrigerant piping. Electronic expansion valves at each indoor unit vary the refrigerant flow to match each zone's load.

Advantages (2020 5d)
  1. High part-load efficiency: inverter compressor runs at exactly the needed capacity.
  2. Individual zone control; up to 40-60 indoor units on one outdoor unit.
  3. Heat recovery: simultaneous heating and cooling, rejected heat is reused.
  4. No ducts or chilled-water pipes; small refrigerant pipes save space; modular, easy to expand.
  5. Quiet indoor units; simple installation in existing buildings.
  6. Individual energy metering possible.

Limitations: high first cost, large refrigerant charge (leak risk in small rooms), limited pipe lengths, fresh air needs a separate system.

Three-pipe heat recovery VRF (2024 7b, 2021 7a)
  • Three pipes run from the outdoor unit: discharge (hot) gas line, suction gas line, and liquid line.
  • An indoor unit in heating takes hot gas from the discharge line, condenses it, and returns liquid to the liquid line.
  • An indoor unit in cooling takes liquid from the liquid line, evaporates it, and returns gas to the suction line.
  • So the heat removed from rooms being cooled is delivered to rooms being heated. The outdoor coil only handles the imbalance. Each indoor unit has a branch selector (solenoid valve) box.
  • Result: COP (coefficient of performance) of heat recovery operation can reach 6-8 when loads balance.
Two-pipe heat recovery VRF (2020 5d)

Only two pipes (high-pressure two-phase line and low-pressure gas line) go from the outdoor unit to a BC (branch) controller. Its gas-liquid separator sends high-pressure gas to heating units and liquid to cooling units, then collects their returns. Fewer pipes and joints than three-pipe.

Multi-split vs VRF (2023 7b, 2021 7b)
Heat pump multi-splitVRF multi-split
Usually fixed-speed or simple inverter compressorInverter compressor(s), capacity modulates 10-100%
2-5 indoor units; each often has its own pipe pair to the outdoor unitUp to ~60 indoor units on one pipe network with branches
All units in the same mode (all cool or all heat)Heat recovery type can heat and cool at the same time
Short pipe lengths (~15-30 m)Long pipes (up to ~150-1000 m total) and large height differences
On/off control, lower part-load efficiencyElectronic expansion valves, precise zone control, higher seasonal efficiency
Cheap, for homes and small officesCostly, for commercial buildings

Remember: VRF = inverter + EEV per unit. Three pipes: hot gas, suction, liquid. Heating unit makes liquid, cooling unit uses it.

B8 Cooling load: components, assumptions, numerical Very likely · 100%Hard

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2024 Q7(c) [15] Two of the wall faces N and W contain double glaze window of a room as shown in figure. If there is no heat gain through other walls, what is the required cooling capacity of the room? Inside: DBT (dry bulb temperature) 43 °C, RH (relative humidity) 55% (as printed). Outside: DBT 43 °C, WBT (wet bulb temperature) 24 °C. U-value of wall, roof and floor 1.78, 1.3, 1.2. ETD (equivalent temperature difference) wall 25 °C, roof 30 °C. SHG 300 W/m², SC (shading coefficient) 0.86. Light 33 W/m² floor. Occupancy 4 (90 W sensible + 40 W latent each). Appliances 600 W sensible + 400 W latent. Infiltration 0.5 ACH (air changes per hour).
  • 2023 Q7(c) [7] What are assumptions should be considered while calculating the cooling load?
  • 2023 Q7(d) [15] Define heating and cooling load. Describe how the cooling load in the form of grand total load on air conditioning system can be evaluated.
  • 2021 Q7(c) [7] What is meant by cooling load? What assumptions behind cooling load design?
  • 2020 Q6(a) [10] What is cooling load? List the main components of cooling load estimation.
Before you start: cooling load

Cooling load = heat that must be removed per second to hold the room at set conditions. Sources: through walls/roof (sun + hot air), windows (sunshine through glass), outside air leaking in or ventilated, and inside: people, lights, equipment. Sensible heat changes temperature; latent heat is moisture.

Cooling load and heating load (2023 7d, 2021 7c, 2020 6a)
  • Cooling load: the rate at which heat must be removed from a space to keep it at the design indoor condition. Peak occurs in the daytime; outdoor conditions and solar radiation change through the day, so it is an unsteady calculation; all internal gains add to it.
  • Heating load: the rate of heat loss from the building in winter that must be supplied. Peak occurs before sunrise; usually calculated as steady state, with no solar gain, neglecting internal gains (conservative).
Assumptions in cooling load design (2023 7c, 2021 7c)
  1. Design outside conditions are taken from long-term statistical weather data for the location, not any one actual year.
  2. Solar load is estimated for clear sky conditions.
  3. Building occupancy is at full design capacity.
  4. All equipment and appliances run at a representative capacity.
  5. Design load is near the maximum, not the absolute maximum (to avoid oversizing).
Components of cooling load (2020 6a)
External loadsFormulaType
Walls, roof, floor, doors (opaque)Q = U A CLTD (or ETD)Sensible
Windows (fenestration)Q = A[Ug(To − Ti) + SHGF (solar heat gain factor)max · SC · CLF (cooling load factor)]Sensible
InfiltrationQs = m cpm(To − Ti), QL = m hfg(Wo − Wi)Both
Bypassed ventilation air, duct gainsQ = m BPF (bypass factor) cpmΔT, m BPF hfgΔWBoth
Internal loads
OccupantsN × sensible/person × CLF; N × latent/personBoth
LightingWatts × utilization factor × ballast factor (1.25 fluorescent) × CLFSensible
Equipment, appliancesWatts × utilization × CLF; latent partBoth

CLTD (cooling load temperature difference)/ETD: equivalent temperature difference that gives the same heat gain as the real combined effect of outdoor temperature, solar radiation and wall heat storage. Depends on orientation, construction, colour, outdoor temp, time, latitude. SC = solar gain through the glass / solar gain through standard clear glass. CLF accounts for the time lag of radiant gains.

Grand total load (2023 7d)

RSH (room sensible heat) = Σ sensible room gains; RLH (room latent heat) = Σ latent room gains; RTH (room total heat) = RSH + RLH
OATH (outside air total heat) = mo(ho − hi) (ventilation load)
GTH (grand total heat) = RTH + OATH (+ safety factor and duct/fan gains, often ×1.1-1.25)
Plant capacity (TR) = GTH / 3.5 kW

Methods: rules of thumb (TR per m²), semi-empirical CLTD/CLF/SHGF method (hand calculation, used in exams), transfer function method and heat balance method (computer).

Numerical (2024 7c): room 5 m × 3 m × 4 m, windows on W and N walls

Assumptions (same as the class 14 example the question is built from): inside 25 °C DBT, 50% RH (the printed "43 °C, 55%" must be a misprint); outside 43 °C DBT, 24 °C WBT; floor over a ventilated basement, so ΔT = 43 − 25 = 18 K; glass U = 3.12 W/m²K (not given; class example value); CLF = 1; ρ = 1.095 kg/m³; Wi = 0.00992, Wo = 0.0107 kg/kg.

Areas (from the sketch: 5 m face is West with 2 × 1.5 m window; 3 m face is North with 1 × 1 m window):

West wall net = 5 × 4 − 3 = 17 m²; North wall net = 3 × 4 − 1 = 11 m²; roof = floor = 5 × 3 = 15 m²; glass = 4 m²; volume = 60 m³

1. Walls: 1.78 × (17 + 11) × 25 = 1246 W (S)

2. Roof: 1.3 × 15 × 30 = 585 W (S)

3. Floor: 1.2 × 15 × 18 = 324 W (S)

4. Glass: 4 × [3.12 × 18 + 300 × 0.86] = 4 × 314.2 = 1257 W (S)

5. Infiltration: m = 1.095 × 0.5 × 60/3600 = 0.00913 kg/s; Qs = 0.00913 × 1021.6 × 18 = 168 W; QL = 0.00913 × 2501 × 103 × (0.0107 − 0.00992) = 18 W

6. People: 4 × 90 = 360 W (S); 4 × 40 = 160 W (L)

7. Lights: 33 × 15 = 495 W (S)

8. Appliances: 600 W (S), 400 W (L)

RSH = 1246 + 585 + 324 + 1257 + 168 + 360 + 495 + 600 = 5035 W; RLH = 18 + 160 + 400 = 578 W

RTH = 5613 W; RSHF (room sensible heat factor) = 5035/5613 = 0.90

Required capacity with safety factor 1.25 = 5613 × 1.25 = 7016 W ≈ 2.0 TR (ton of refrigeration (3.5 kW))

Remember: Opaque UA·ETD, glass A(UΔT + SHGF·SC), infiltration m cΔT + m hfgΔW, people S+L, lights, appliances. Sum × 1.25.

B3 Summer AC with ventilation air and bypass factor (numerical) Very likely · 90%Hard

Past-paper questions · Must study

  • 2024 Q5(c) [15] A refrigeration plant is shown in figure. Determine: (i) Dehumidified air quantity, (ii) Sensible and latent heat gain due to outside air, (iii) Total refrigeration load of the plant.
  • 2023 Q5(d) [11] Describe a summer air-conditioning with ventilation air-bypass factor.
  • 2021 Q5(c) [15] The room sensible heat gain and latent heat gain of a conditioned space are 40 kW and 15 kW respectively. The inside design conditions are 25 °C DBT (dry bulb temperature) and 55% RH (relative humidity). The return air is mixed with outside air before entering the cooling coil in the ratio of 3:1 by weight. Assuming the bypass factor of the cooling coil is 0.13, determine: (i) Apparatus dew point (ADP), (ii) Ventilation air in cmm, (iii) Total refrigeration load of the plant.
Before you start: the summer AC numerical in plain words

Room air (i) is mixed with some hot outside air (o) for freshness: the mix (1) is found by mass-weighted average. The cooling coil cools it towards its surface temperature, the apparatus dew point (ADP), but a fraction X of air passes through untouched: the bypass factor. So coil exit t2 = ADP (apparatus dew point) + X(t1 − ADP).

Supply air must pick up the room sensible heat: m = RSH (room sensible heat) / [cp(ti − t2)]. The coil must remove room load + outside air load.

Theory (2023 5d): summer AC with ventilation air and bypass factor
  1. Outside air o (hot, humid) mixes with room return air i in a fixed ratio to give state 1 (mixing line, by mass ratio).
  2. Mixed air passes over the coil with coil ADP t′s. Because of bypass factor X, it leaves at 2, not at ADP: t2 = tADP + X(t1 − tADP). Line 1-S′ is the GSHF line (apparatus condition line).
  3. Supply air 2 enters the room and picks up RSH and RLH (room latent heat) along the RSHF line 2-i.
  4. Load on coil = room load + ventilation (outside air) load: GTH (grand total heat) = RTH (room total heat) + OATH (outside air total heat).

(ma)d = RSH / [cpm(ti − tADP)(1 − X)] = RSH / [cpm(ti − ts)]
OASH (outside air sensible heat) = mocpm(to − ti)   OALH (outside air latent heat) = mohfg(wo − wi)   OATH = mo(ho − hi)
GTH = RSH + RLH + OATH = ma(h1 − h2);   GSHF = TSH (total sensible heat)/GTH

Numerical 1 (2024 5c): RSH 20 kW, RLH 5 kW, room 25 °C / 50%, OA 43 °C DBT / 27.5 °C WBT (wet bulb temperature), ADP 12 °C, X = 0.13, 3:1

Chart values (same as the class 06 example): outside wo = 17 g/kg, ho = 87.5 kJ/kg, vo = 0.922 m³/kg; inside wi = 10 g/kg, hi = 50.8 kJ/kg; cpm = 1.02, hfg = 2500.

3:1 by weight → return 75%, outside 25%.

Mixed: t1 = 0.75(25) + 0.25(43) = 29.5 °C; w1 = 0.75(10) + 0.25(17) = 11.75 g/kg; h1 = 0.75(50.8) + 0.25(87.5) = 60.0 kJ/kg

Coil exit: ts = 12 + 0.13(29.5 − 12) = 14.3 °C

(i) Dehumidified air (ma)d = 20 / [1.02(25 − 14.3)] = 1.83 kg/s (≈1.83 × 0.86 × 60 ≈ 94 m³/min)

Outside air mo = 0.25 × 1.83 = 0.457 kg/s (= 0.457 × 0.922 = 0.42 m³/s)

(ii) OASH = 0.457 × 1.02 × (43 − 25) = 8.4 kW; OALH = 0.457 × 2500 × (0.017 − 0.010) = 8.0 kW

OATH = 0.457 × (87.5 − 50.8) = 16.8 kW

(iii) Total load GTH = RTH + OATH = (20 + 5) + 16.8 = 41.8 kW ≈ 11.9 TR (ton of refrigeration (3.5 kW))

Numerical 2 (2021 5c): RSH 40 kW, RLH 15 kW, room 25 °C / 55%, OA 35 °C / 65% RH (written on the paper), 3:1, X = 0.13

Chart: outside wo = 23.4 g/kg, ho = 95.2 kJ/kg, vo = 0.905 m³/kg; inside wi = 10.9 g/kg, hi = 53.0 kJ/kg

Mixed: t1 = 0.75(25) + 0.25(35) = 27.5 °C; w1 = 0.75(10.9) + 0.25(23.4) = 14.05 g/kg

(i) ADP by trial: supply state 2 must satisfy both the bypass relation and the room ratio RSH/RLH = 40/15 = 2.67:

t2 = tADP + 0.13(27.5 − tADP),   w2 = wADP + 0.13(14.05 − wADP),   1.0216(25 − t2) / [2501(wi − w2)] = 2.67

Try tADP = 11.5 °C (wADP = 8.45 g/kg): t2 = 13.6 °C, w2 = 9.18 g/kg → ratio = 1.0216(11.4)/(2501 × 0.00172) = 2.67 ✓

ADP ≈ 11.5 °C

(ma)d = 40 / [1.0216(25 − 13.6)] = 3.42 kg/s; mo = 0.25 × 3.42 = 0.854 kg/s

(ii) Ventilation air = 0.854 × 0.905 × 60 = 46.4 m³/min (cmm)

OATH = 0.854(95.2 − 53.0) = 36.1 kW

(iii) Total load = 40 + 15 + 36.1 = 91.1 kW ≈ 25.9 TR

Values were read from moist-air equations at 101.325 kPa; chart readings may differ by about 2-3%. If your copy of the 2021 paper has no outside condition, state "assumed 35 °C DBT, 65% RH" before solving.

Remember: Mix → coil (ts = ADP + X(t1 − ADP)) → room. m = RSH/[1.02(ti − ts)]. Total = RTH + mo(ho − hi).

Same answer, step by step with reasons
Step (write this)Why / what it means
Mix 3:1 → t1 = 0.75 × 25 + 0.25 × 43 = 29.5 °C; h1 = 0.75 × 50.8 + 0.25 × 87.5 = 60.0 kJ/kgMixing = weighted average by mass (3 parts return, 1 part outside).
Coil exit t2 = ADP + X(t1 − ADP) = 12 + 0.13 × 17.5 = 14.3 °C13 % of air bypasses the coil uncooled.
ma = RSH / [cpm(ti − t2)] = 20/(1.02 × 10.7) = 1.83 kg/sSupply air warms from 14.3 to 25 °C absorbing the room sensible heat.
mo = 0.25 × 1.83 = 0.457 kg/sOutside-air share.
OATH = mo(ho − hi) = 0.457 × 36.7 = 16.8 kWLoad from cooling the outside air down to room condition.
Coil load = RSH + RLH + OATH = 20 + 5 + 16.8 = 41.8 kW ≈ 11.9 TRRoom load plus fresh-air load; divide by 3.5 for TR.

Memory trick: "Mix, Bypass, Mass, Load".

B10 Duct design rules, outlets, dampers, diffusers Likely · 60%Easy

Past-paper questions · Good to have

  • 2023 Q8(b) [7] What factors should be considered while selecting the location of supply air outlets?
  • 2023 Q7(a) [6] Write down the functions of the following: (i) Dampers; (ii) Diffusers.
  • 2021 Q8(c) [6] What are the general rules for duct design?
  • 2021 Q8(b) [8] What factors should be considered to locating the supply air outlets and return air inlets?
  • 2020 Q6(b) [8] What are the general rules of duct design?
Before you start: duct design rules

Keep air speed moderate (noise), use gradual bends and transitions (less pressure loss), dampers to balance flow, and diffusers/grilles that spread air without draughts.

Not in the uploaded slides; standard textbook points.

General rules for duct design (2021 8c, 2020 6b)
  1. Run ducts as straight and short as possible; avoid sharp bends (use turning vanes or radius elbows, R/W ≥ 1.25).
  2. Keep the aspect ratio of rectangular ducts low (≤ 4:1, ideally near 1:1 to 3:1).
  3. Use velocities within limits to control noise: main ducts ~5-8 m/s in residences, up to 10-12 m/s in commercial buildings; branches lower.
  4. Change cross-section gradually (taper angle ≤ 15-20°) to reduce dynamic losses.
  5. Seal joints to limit leakage; insulate ducts through unconditioned spaces.
  6. Provide dampers for balancing and fire dampers where required; allow access for cleaning.
  7. Balance the system so each outlet gets its design airflow; keep the longest run's pressure loss reasonable.
Factors for locating supply outlets and return inlets (2023 8b, 2021 8b)
  • Throw, spread and drop of the air jet so air reaches the occupied zone at 0.15-0.25 m/s without draught.
  • Location of heat sources and loads: put outlets near windows and outer walls to offset gains/losses.
  • Ceiling height and room shape; furniture and obstructions.
  • Avoid short-circuiting: returns placed away from supplies so air sweeps the room.
  • Noise level and appearance; mixing and temperature uniformity; cooling vs heating mode (cool air from high level, warm from low level).
  • Returns: near the floor or at high level for hot air, away from people, sized for low velocity (< 2-4 m/s).
Functions of dampers and diffusers (2023 7a)
  • Dampers: control or shut off airflow in ducts: volume control and system balancing, mixing outdoor and return air, fire and smoke isolation (fire dampers), backdraft prevention.
  • Diffusers: supply outlets that spread air into the room in a pattern, mix it quickly with room air, and lower its velocity so that there is no draught or noise.

Remember: Duct: short, straight, low aspect ratio, sealed, balanced. Outlets: throw, spread, no short-circuit.

B11 Sol-air temperature, window solar gain, infiltration Possible · 50%Medium

Past-paper questions · Good to have

  • 2023 Q8(a) [4] What is meant by sol-air temperature?
  • 2021 Q7(d) [8] What is sol-air temperature? How to estimate the solar heat gain through building window?
  • 2021 Q8(a) [7] What is infiltration? How to estimate infiltration rate using Crack method?
Before you start: solar gains

A sunlit wall acts as if the outside air were hotter: sol-air temperature = Tair + αq/ho. Windows let sunshine straight in. Infiltration (air leaking through cracks) adds both sensible and latent load.

Sol-air temperature (2023 8a, 2021 7d)

The sol-air temperature is the fictitious outdoor air temperature that, with no solar radiation, would give the same heat flow into an outside surface as the actual combination of outdoor air temperature, incident solar radiation and long-wave sky exchange.

tsa = to + α It/ho − εΔR/ho  (α = absorptivity, It = total solar radiation, ho = outside film coefficient; last term ≈ 4 K for roofs, 0 for walls)

Heat gain through a wall or roof then is Q = U A (tsa − ti) (steady), and CLTD (cooling load temperature difference)/ETD values are derived from it.

Solar heat gain through a window (2021 7d)

Qglass = A[Uglass(To − Ti) + SHGF (solar heat gain factor)max × SC (shading coefficient) × CLF (cooling load factor)]

  • First term: conduction through the glass.
  • SHGF: solar heat gain factor from tables (orientation, month, hour, latitude).
  • SC: shading coefficient = gain through this glass / gain through standard clear glass; depends on glass type and blinds.
  • CLF: cooling load factor for the time lag of radiant heat stored in room surfaces.
Infiltration and crack method (2021 8a)

Infiltration is the uncontrolled flow of outdoor air into a building through cracks around windows and doors and other unintended openings (air leakage), caused by wind and stack pressure.

Crack method: infiltration rate = (crack length) × (leakage per metre of crack) for the windward windows and doors.

V̇ = Σ (Lcrack × qper m) m³/h, where q depends on window type and the wind speed (pressure difference), from tables

Then Qs = m cpm(To − Ti) and QL = m hfg(Wo − Wi), with m = ρV̇. The simpler air change method uses V̇ = ACH (air changes per hour) × room volume / 3600 m³/s (used in the 2024 cooling load problem).

Remember: Sol-air = air temp + absorbed sun ÷ ho. Crack method = crack length × leakage per metre.
